meta.description: Song-misattribution backlog for /who-recorded/. A cover mistaken for the ORIGINAL recording. Managed by tools/songs.js — do not hand-edit counts. Lifecycle: queued → selected → ingested (or dropped).

songs.title: After Midnight
songs.whyNotable: A signature Clapton song that most listeners assume he originated. J.J. Cale wrote and first recorded it, released November 1966 as a Liberty single b/w "Slow Motion". Clapton recorded his in January 1970 at Island Studios and Polydor released it in October 1970; it reached No. 18 on the Hot 100. The clinching detail: Clapton's success prompted Cale to RE-record his own song for 1971's Naturally, and that re-recording — not the 1966 original — is the Cale version most people have heard, which is a second layer of the same confusion.
caveats: J.J. Cale re-recorded his own song for Naturally (1971) after Clapton's 1970 hit, releasing it as a single in 1972 (No. 42). The Cale version most listeners have heard is therefore not the 1966 Liberty original.

songs.title: Angel from Montgomery
songs.whyNotable: Prine wrote it and recorded it for his self-titled 1971 debut on Atlantic. Raitt cut it for Streetlights in 1974, and Wikipedia notes hers is the version that 'first attained wide recognition for the song'. Because Raitt sang it in a woman's voice — and kept it in her live set for fifty years — it reads to most listeners as a Bonnie Raitt song rather than a John Prine record.

songs.title: At Last
songs.whyNotable: Etta James's Argo recording is so completely hers that the wedding-DJ world treats her as its author. It is a Mack Gordon and Harry Warren film song written for Sun Valley Serenade in 1941, and Glenn Miller's orchestra had the hit — the May 20, 1942 studio version with Ray Eberle reached number 2. Note for the editor: this one runs against the vein's usual direction (big-band original, soul cover), but the who-recorded-it-first axis is identical.
caveats: the 1941/1942 distinction matters. Glenn Miller's orchestra performed it in Sun Valley Serenade in 1941 (the vocal was cut from the release print; Pat Friday dubbed Lynn Bari), made unreleased recordings in 1941, and the vocal arrangement resurfaced in Orchestra Wives in 1942. The RELEASED studio recording with Ray Eberle is May 20, 1942 on RCA Victor, which is the year given above.

songs.title: Black Betty
songs.originalArtist: James "Iron Head" Baker and Clear Rock
songs.originalLabel: Library of Congress field recording (John and Alan Lomax)
songs.whyNotable: The first known recording was made in December 1933 by the convicts Iron Head and Clear Rock at Central State Farm, Sugar Land, Texas, captured in the field by John and Alan Lomax for the Library of Congress. Lead Belly cut the commercial version in New York in April 1939 for Musicraft, as part of a medley on Negro Sinful Songs. Ram Jam's hard-rock arrangement, released June 1977, reached No. 18 in the US, No. 7 in the UK and No. 3 in Australia — and is now so dominant that the song's origin as an African-American work song is invisible to most listeners.
caveats: Lead Belly is the usual answer and is wrong. The earliest known recording is the December 1933 Lomax field recording of Iron Head and Clear Rock at Sugar Land, Texas; Lead Belly's commercial Musicraft version is 1939.

songs.title: Blue Velvet
songs.whyNotable: Vinton's Epic recording (made 27 May 1963, released 2 August 1963) spent three weeks at number one and was cemented by David Lynch's 1986 film — it is his song in the public mind. It is a 1950 Wayne/Morris composition with a tangled 1951 recording history, and by the time Vinton got to it there had already been charting versions by Tony Bennett (1951) and the Clovers (1955, number 14 R&B). See the contested note: the question of which 1951 record came first is genuinely knotty and is the best material on this page.
caveats: the "original" is genuinely disputed. Wikipedia says Tony Bennett recorded it first, on 17 July 1951 (Columbia, released 21 September 1951), but that Arthur Prysock's Decca version, cut about a week after Bennett's session, "evidently was the first version released, in August 1951." First recorded and first released are different artists. I have listed Prysock as originalArtist on the first-released reading; the page should present both and say which test it is applying.

songs.title: Call Me the Breeze
songs.whyNotable: Cale recorded it in 1970 and released it on his debut album Naturally (25 October 1971). Lynyrd Skynyrd recorded their version in January 1974 for Second Helping and made it a Southern-rock staple, re-recording it live for One More from the Road in 1976. The boogie-piano Skynyrd arrangement is so identified with the band that the song is widely assumed to be theirs — the second major case, after 'Cocaine', of a Cale original being absorbed by its cover.

songs.title: City of New Orleans
songs.whyNotable: Goodman wrote it in 1970 and recorded it for his self-titled 1971 album on Buddah. Guthrie's version, released June 1972 from Hobo's Lullaby, reached No. 18 on the Hot 100 and No. 4 Easy Listening, and hit No. 1 in New Zealand in 1973. Willie Nelson's 1984 version topped the country chart and won Goodman a posthumous Grammy for Best Country Song. Guthrie's name and Woody Guthrie's shadow make the song read as an inherited American folk standard rather than a Chicago songwriter's copyright.

songs.title: Cocaine
songs.whyNotable: Cale wrote and recorded it for his album Troubadour, released September 1976 on Shelter Records. Clapton cut it for Slowhand in 1977, where it became one of his signature numbers and was issued as the B-side of 'Lay Down Sally'. Clapton's version so completely displaced Cale's in public memory that the song is routinely listed among Clapton's own compositions; Cale's Tulsa-sound original is the record almost nobody has heard.

songs.title: Devil with a Blue Dress On
songs.whyNotable: Mitch Ryder's frantic 1966 medley with 'Good Golly, Miss Molly' hit number 4 and is treated as the source of the song. Shorty Long wrote it with Motown A&R chief Mickey Stevenson and released it as his debut single in 1964, at a far slower tempo; it reached number 26 R&B. The speed is Ryder's invention — the song is not.

songs.title: Different Drum
songs.coverArtist: The Stone Poneys featuring Linda Ronstadt
songs.whyNotable: Nesmith wrote it in 1964, and the bluegrass group The Greenbriar Boys recorded it first, on their 1966 album Better Late than Never!. The Stone Poneys featuring Linda Ronstadt released their baroque-pop arrangement on Capitol in September 1967; it reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became Ronstadt's first hit. Double misattribution: listeners assume Ronstadt originated it, and those who know better usually credit the Monkees rather than a bluegrass band.

songs.title: Don't Leave Me This Way
songs.writer: Kenneth Gamble, Leon Huff and Cary Gilbert
songs.whyNotable: Two different singers had number ones with this and neither cut it first. Gamble, Huff and Cary Gilbert's original was an album track on Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes' 1975 Wake Up Everybody. Thelma Houston's 1976 Tamla version topped the Hot 100 and won a Grammy; the Communards' 1986 version spent four weeks at UK number one and was the best-selling British single of the year. Both famous 'originals' are covers.

songs.title: Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood
songs.writer: Bennie Benjamin, Horace Ott and Sol Marcus
songs.whyNotable: Rolling Stone placed the Animals' version at No. 322 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time, and the song is routinely treated as an Animals original alongside their other signature reworkings. Nina Simone recorded the first version in October 1964 for Broadway-Blues-Ballads on Philips; the Animals released theirs on 29 January 1965 in the UK, reaching No. 3 UK, No. 15 US and No. 4 in Canada. Written by Bennie Benjamin, Horace Ott and Sol Marcus. A third layer: Santa Esmeralda's 1977 disco version (US No. 15, No. 1 in Italy and West Germany) is itself widely assumed to be covering the Animals rather than Simone.

songs.title: Dueling Banjos
songs.originalArtist: Arthur "Guitar Boogie" Smith with Don Reno (as "Feudin' Banjos")
songs.whyNotable: The rare misattribution where the film industry made the same mistake the public did, and lost in court for it. Arthur Smith composed the piece in 1954 and first recorded it in 1955 as 'Feudin' Banjos', playing four-string plectrum banjo against Don Reno's five-string. The Eric Weissberg and Steve Mandell arrangement in Deliverance (1972) is what the world knows; the December 1972 single was credited to Weissberg alone, and the filmmakers did not acknowledge Smith as composer at all. Smith sued, won, and received songwriting credit plus royalties. The Weissberg-Mandell recording went to No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1973 and took a Grammy for Best Country Instrumental Performance in 1974 — awards for a tune whose author had to litigate to be named.
caveats: the credit was contested in court, not just in public memory. The December 1972 single was credited to Eric Weissberg alone although Steve Mandell arranged and performed it with him, and Arthur Smith received no composer credit from the filmmakers until he sued and won songwriting credit plus royalties.

songs.title: Evil Ways
songs.whyNotable: Santana's first US Top 40 hit — number nine on the Hot 100 the week of 21 March 1970 — and one of the tracks that made the Woodstock reputation. Wikipedia: "It was written by Clarence 'Sonny' Henry and originally recorded by jazz percussionist Willie Bobo on his 1967 album Bobo Motion." Santana did not record it until May 1969. The Latin-jazz original is genuinely obscure, which makes the misattribution near-total rather than merely common.

songs.title: For Once in My Life
songs.whyNotable: Everyone files this under Stevie Wonder, whose Tamla single came out on October 15, 1968. He recorded it in summer 1967 and Berry Gordy shelved it — by which point Jean DuShon had already released it on Chess's Cadet label in October 1966 and Tony Bennett had charted with it in 1967. Two earlier recordings exist still: see contested.
caveats: Jean DuShon (Cadet, October 1966) is the first RELEASED version, not the first recorded. Wikipedia records a Connie Haines recording made at Motown in July 1965 that stayed unreleased until 2015, and a Barbara McNair recording made in October 1965 and issued on an album in November 1966. Whoever the page names, it is not Stevie Wonder.

songs.title: Georgia on My Mind
songs.whyNotable: Charles took it to number one on the Hot 100 in 1960 (ABC-Paramount, recorded May 1960 for The Genius Hits the Road) and it became Georgia's state song largely because of him — most listeners assume it is his, and many assume he wrote it. Wikipedia: "Carmichael first recorded 'Georgia on My Mind', with Bix Beiderbecke on cornet, in New York City on September 15, 1930." Composer, cornetist, decade and idiom all differ from the version people know.

songs.title: Gloria
songs.writer: Umberto Tozzi and Giancarlo Bigazzi; English translation by Jonathan King
songs.whyNotable: Branigan's is the version that reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 (27 November 1982, held off by Lionel Richie's "Truly") and it is treated as her signature song outright. Wikipedia records it as a 1979 Italian recording by Umberto Tozzi, written by Tozzi with Giancarlo Bigazzi, released on CGD. The Tozzi page adds that Branigan worked with Greg Mathieson — the arranger and keyboardist on Tozzi's own version — to give it what she called "an American kick", which is about as direct a line back to the original as a cover gets.

songs.title: Goo Goo Muck
songs.whyNotable: The most recent and most measurable case in this vein. The Cramps cut it at A&M Studios in January 1981 for Psychedelic Jungle; the original is a 1962 record by Ronnie Cook and the Gaylads. The dance scene in Netflix's Wednesday sent it viral, and the numbers are documented: US on-demand streams went from 2,500 to over 134,000, and Spotify streams rose 9,500 percent. Every one of those listeners arrived at a 1962 song via a 1981 cover in a streaming series, and the near-universal shorthand in the coverage that followed was 'the Cramps song'. One critic went as far as saying the moment 'may have single-handedly revived' goth subculture for Gen Z.

songs.title: Green, Green Grass of Home
songs.whyNotable: Putman's song was first recorded by Johnny Darrell, released as his debut single on United Artists in May 1965. Porter Wagoner followed in July 1965 (No. 4 country, RCA Victor) and Jerry Lee Lewis cut it for Country Songs for City Folks. Jones learned it from the Lewis record and released his Decca version on 28 October 1966; it spent seven weeks at No. 1 in the UK and reached No. 11 in the US. Outside Nashville the song is simply a Tom Jones number — the third-hand chain from Darrell through Lewis to Jones is invisible.

songs.title: Heartbeats
songs.whyNotable: A pure advert-driven misattribution, and the chart record proves the sync did the work rather than the song. The Knife released it on 27 December 2002 on Rabid and V2; it reached No. 26 in Sweden and No. 119 on the UK Singles Chart. González's acoustic cover sat quietly on his 2003 debut Veneer until Sony's Bravia commercial — 250,000 coloured balls bouncing down Russian Hill in San Francisco — put it on television in November 2005. Reissued as a single on 9 January 2006, the cover hit No. 9 in the UK, No. 6 in Scotland, and went platinum in the UK and Denmark. An electro-pop record that barely registered became, for most of its audience, a solo acoustic song by an Argentine-Swedish guitarist.

songs.title: Hey Joe
songs.whyNotable: Near-universal belief that Hendrix wrote and originated it — it was his debut single and is treated as a Hendrix signature. Wikipedia has The Leaves issuing the first commercial version in November/December 1965 on Mira; Hendrix recorded 23 October 1966 and Polydor released it in the UK on 16 December 1966, reaching No. 6 in January 1967. The Leaves' 1966 re-cut hit No. 31 on the Hot 100 and is per Wikipedia the only version ever to reach the US Top 40 — Hendrix's failed to chart in the US. Love's version (recorded January 1966, released April 1966 on Elektra) sits between them. Authorship itself is contested: Billy Roberts copyrighted it in 1962, Dino Valenti also copyrighted it in Los Angeles, and Len Partridge claimed co-authorship dating to 1956.
caveats: authorship is disputed three ways: Billy Roberts copyrighted it in 1962, Dino Valenti separately copyrighted it in Los Angeles, and Len Partridge claimed he co-wrote it with Roberts in 1956. Roberts performed it in the late 1950s and early 1960s but no commercial recording by him preceded The Leaves. The Leaves also cut three versions; the November/December 1965 release flopped and the third, in 1966, was the hit.

songs.title: Hush
songs.whyNotable: Deep Purple's debut hit and, for hard-rock audiences, an unambiguously Deep Purple song — the Kula Shaker revival in 1997 (UK No. 2) reinforced that, since it was read as a Deep Purple cover rather than a Billy Joe Royal cover. Royal recorded it on 12 July 1967 and Columbia released it that September; it only reached No. 52 on the Hot 100, while Deep Purple's 1968 version hit No. 4. Written by Joe South. The original's commercial obscurity is exactly why the misattribution holds.

songs.title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine
songs.whyNotable: Marvin Gaye's is one of the most famous records Motown ever made, and it is the third version of the song. The Miracles cut it first on August 6, 1966 and Berry Gordy vetoed the release; Gaye recorded his over five sessions between February 3 and April 10, 1967 and Gordy shelved that too; Gladys Knight & the Pips recorded theirs on June 17, 1967 and got out first, as a single on September 28, 1967. Gaye's did not appear as a single until October 30, 1968.
caveats: three-way, and the three orderings disagree. Wikipedia states the Miracles made the first known recording on August 6, 1966 (unreleased until the Special Occasion album in August 1968); Marvin Gaye recorded second, February 3 to April 10, 1967, but released third, October 30, 1968; Gladys Knight & the Pips recorded third, June 17, 1967, but were the FIRST RELEASED, September 28, 1967. The record proposed above names the Miracles as first-recorded, which is what the source says; an editor may prefer to name Gladys Knight as first-released instead.

songs.title: I Just Want to Make Love to You
songs.whyNotable: Etta James's reading is the one the public knows, and the 1996 Diet Coke advertising campaign made it a hit in its own right decades later — it charted at No. 7 in Ireland and No. 27 in the Netherlands off the back of the ad, which cemented it as "an Etta James song". Muddy Waters recorded it first in 1954, released on Chess as "Just Make Love to Me", reaching No. 4 on Billboard's R&B Best Sellers chart. Willie Dixon wrote it. The British-invasion leg is real too: the Rolling Stones cut it for their 1964 debut album and Foghat's 1972 version was their first chart single (No. 83), later bettered by an edited live version in 1977 (No. 33).

songs.title: I Put a Spell on You
songs.writer: Screamin' Jay Hawkins and Herb Slotkin
songs.whyNotable: Hawkins recorded it on 12 September 1956 and Okeh released it that October; it sold over a million copies but 'failed to make the Billboard pop or R&B charts' because radio banned it for the screaming delivery. So there is no hit original standing in the way — for the cohort raised on Hocus Pocus (1993), the song simply IS the Sanderson Sisters number, performed by Bette Midler at the Halloween party in an arrangement produced by Marc Shaiman. The film's annual-rewatch status makes the exposure enormous and repeating: Freeform's first week of Hocus Pocus airings averaged 8.2 million viewers in 2018. Nina Simone (1965), the Alan Price Set (1966, UK No. 9) and Creedence Clearwater Revival (1968) all cover it too, but none of those placed it in front of a generation of children every October.

songs.title: I Will Follow Him
songs.writer: Franck Pourcel (as J. W. Stole) and Paul Mauriat (as Del Roma); French lyrics by Jacques Plante
songs.whyNotable: A US number one that made March the youngest female artist to top the Hot 100 — and, after Sister Act, one of the most recognisable songs in American pop. It began as a French instrumental: Wikipedia states "The song was first recorded by Franck Pourcel as an instrumental, and was released in 1961" under the title "Chariot". Petula Clark cut a French vocal version as "Chariot" in 1962. March did not record the English version until 7 January 1963, at RCA Victor Studios in New York; RCA released it on 22 January 1963. The song had two lives in French before it had any in English.

songs.title: I'm Gonna Make You Love Me
songs.creditedTo: Diana Ross & the Supremes and The Temptations
songs.writer: Kenneth Gamble, Leon Huff and Jerry Ross
songs.coverArtist: Diana Ross & the Supremes and The Temptations
songs.whyNotable: The November 1968 Motown summit meeting between the Supremes and the Temptations sold 900,000 copies in a fortnight and is the version everybody knows — and it is the third recording. Dee Dee Warwick, Dionne's sister, cut Gamble and Huff's song for Mercury in 1966, and Madeline Bell had already taken it to number 26 on the Hot 100 in April 1968.

songs.title: In the Mood
songs.writer: Wingy Manone (composer), Andy Razaf (lyrics), Joe Garland (arranger)
songs.whyNotable: The single most Glenn-Miller-identified record in existence — recorded 1 August 1939 at RCA Victor Studios in New York, released 15 September 1939 on Bluebird (HMV in the UK). Wikipedia: "The first recording under the name 'In the Mood' was released by Edgar Hayes and his Orchestra in 1938", as the B-side of "Stardust" on Decca. And the riff is older still — see the contested note on Wingy Manone's "Tar Paper Stomp".
caveats: Edgar Hayes and His Orchestra (Decca, 1938) is, per Wikipedia, "the first recording under the name 'In the Mood'", but the melody is older: Wingy Manone "recorded 'Tar Paper Stomp' on August 28, 1930, in Richmond, Indiana, and released it as a 78 single for Champion Records", and Manone is credited as composer on "In the Mood". So the earliest recording of the tune is 1930 under a different title, nine years before Glenn Miller — that is the strongest fact in the candidate and should carry the caveat that it is a different title, not a different take.

songs.title: Istanbul (Not Constantinople)
songs.whyNotable: Written by Jimmy Kennedy and Nat Simon in 1953 and first recorded by the Canadian vocal quartet The Four Lads on 12 August 1953, released by Columbia as catalogue 40082; it entered the Billboard charts on 24 October 1953, peaked at No. 10 and became the group's first gold record. Nobody under sixty knows that. They Might Be Giants released their faster version on 14 May 1990 from Flood, and it only reached No. 61 on the UK Singles Chart — so the record itself did not drive this. The television placements did: the video ran in the first season of MTV's Liquid Television, and the version soundtracked a 1991 Tiny Toon Adventures music-video segment ('Tiny Toon Music Television') that put it in front of a generation of children, with a later run on The Simpsons ('Mobile Homer', 2005). The result is a widespread belief that TMBG wrote it.

songs.title: It Must Be Love
songs.whyNotable: Madness's most-played ballad is not a Madness song. Labi Siffre wrote and released it in 1971 on Pye, reaching number 14 in the UK in January 1972 — a real hit, but a decade earlier and in a different genre, and Siffre remains a name most people who can hum the Madness version cannot place. The cover was issued as a standalone single in late 1981 and reached number four in the UK, then number 33 on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 1983, and climbed to number six in the UK again on 1992 reissue. Three chart runs under the Madness name against one under Siffre's is roughly how the misattribution got built.

songs.title: It's in His Kiss (The Shoop Shoop Song)
songs.whyNotable: Cher's 1990 Mermaids hit is usually 'corrected' to Betty Everett's 1964 Vee-Jay record — and that correction is wrong too. Merry Clayton, in her first credited single, released Rudy Clark's song on Capitol on June 10, 1963, produced by Jack Nitzsche with Hal Blaine on drums, and it went nowhere. Vee-Jay only bolted the 'Shoop Shoop Song' title onto Everett's single to tell it apart from a rival version.
caveats: the usual 'correction' to Betty Everett (Vee-Jay, 1964) is itself wrong: Merry Clayton's Capitol single came out June 10, 1963. A third contender, Ramona King on Warner Bros., was released in February 1964, the week BEFORE Everett's, which is the actual reason Vee-Jay retitled Everett's record 'The Shoop Shoop Song'. Three claimants inside nine months.

songs.title: Leaving on a Jet Plane
songs.whyNotable: Denver wrote it under the title 'Babe I Hate to Go' and first recorded it in 1966 for his demo record John Denver Sings; producer Milt Okun talked him into the new title in 1967. Peter, Paul and Mary recorded it for Album 1700 in 1967 and released it as a single in September 1969, taking it to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Denver's own RCA re-recording, issued October 1969 from Rhymes & Reasons, failed to chart — so the trio's hit is what the public remembers, even though Denver's own version came first by three years.

songs.title: Lili Marleen
songs.writer: Hans Leip (words, written as a poem in 1915); Norbert Schultze (music, 1938)
songs.whyNotable: Dietrich's name has swallowed this song in the English-speaking world, but Wikipedia is explicit: "it was set to music in 1938 and was first recorded by Lale Andersen in 1939 as 'Das Mädchen unter der Laterne' ('The Girl under the Lantern')" on HMV — under a different title, in German, by a different woman. Dietrich recorded hers in 1944 for the US Office of Strategic Services; it was not released commercially until 1945, on Decca. The German original is six years older than the version most people think is the original.

songs.title: Madness
songs.whyNotable: A band covering a song with the band's own name on it is the strongest possible setup for misattribution, and this is that case. Prince Buster's ska recording dates from 1963, from I Feel the Spirit; the north London group formed in 1976 took their name from it and recorded their version for One Step Beyond..., released 19 October 1979 on Stiff. The album's track listing credits the song to Cecil Campbell — Buster's real name — alongside 'One Step Beyond', making the debut album two Prince Buster covers deep. Listeners who assume a self-titled song must be self-written have the causality exactly backwards.

songs.title: Mah Nà Mah Nà
songs.whyNotable: Almost everyone who knows this tune knows it as a Muppets original, and it is not one — it is a cue Italian composer Piero Umiliani wrote and recorded in 1968 for the soundtrack of the exploitation documentary Svezia, inferno e paradiso (Sweden: Heaven and Hell). The Muppet version premiered on Sesame Street's fourteenth episode on 27 November 1969 (Jim Henson, Frank Oz and Loretta Long) and on The Ed Sullivan Show three days later, then became a signature act on the premiere episode of The Muppet Show in 1976. The reversal is the best detail on the page: the television exposure drove Umiliani's OWN original recording to No. 8 in the UK in 1977, nine years after he cut it — the man who wrote it charted as though he were the cover act.
caveats: an inverted case worth writing up as such: the Muppet Show exposure drove Piero Umiliani's OWN 1968 original to No. 8 in the UK in 1977, while The Muppet Show soundtrack album went to No. 1. The composer charted on the back of the cover that displaced him.

songs.title: Man of Constant Sorrow
songs.writer: Traditional American folk song, author uncertain
songs.whyNotable: A film invented a band, and the band ended up owning a song older than commercial country music. The Soggy Bottom Boys are fictional — the O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000) recording is Dan Tyminski on lead vocal with Harley Allen and Pat Enright, arranged from the Stanley Brothers' reading. The earliest commercially released recording is Emry Arthur's, made 18 January 1928 for Vocalion, with Arthur singing and playing guitar alongside banjoist Dock Boggs. The film version won a CMA Single of the Year (2001), a Grammy (2002) and IBMA Song of the Year (2001), reached No. 35 on Hot Country Songs and had sold over a million copies by November 2016 — an award record for a 'group' that does not exist, performing a song no one alive wrote.
caveats: Emry Arthur's 18 January 1928 Vocalion side is the earliest COMMERCIALLY RELEASED recording, but Wikipedia notes Dick Burnett recorded the song for Columbia in 1927 and that version was never released. So the usual 'first recording' answer is only first-issued. Authorship is separately uncertain: the song is traditional and Wikipedia does not settle a writer.

songs.title: Midnight Train to Georgia
songs.whyNotable: Gladys Knight's signature song — a Billboard number one in October 1973 and a 2026 National Recording Registry pick — reached her second-hand. Cissy Houston, Whitney's mother, recorded it for Janus first, and it was her producer Sonny Limbo who asked Jim Weatherly to let him change the title from 'Midnight Plane to Houston'. Weatherly's publisher then forwarded the Houston version to the Pips.
caveats: Cissy Houston (Janus, 1973) is the first recording under this title, but Jim Weatherly wrote and recorded it first as 'Midnight Plane to Houston' for Jimmy Bowen's Amos Records. Wikipedia gives NO year for the Weatherly recording, so no year is asserted here and none should be added without a source; a search result mentioned a 1972 RCA Victor self-titled album but that was not confirmed on a page I fetched.

songs.title: Misirlou
songs.writer: Traditional Eastern Mediterranean folk melody, composer unknown; Nicholas Roubanis credited himself as composer on a 1941 jazz arrangement and, unchallenged, remains the official worldwide credit
songs.whyNotable: The textbook case for this vein. Dick Dale's staccato surf-guitar version was released 21 April 1962 on Deltone Records, and Wikipedia records no chart placing for it — it was a regional surf record, not a national hit. What made it the version a whole generation met first was Pulp Fiction (1994), where it is 'prominently featured over the opening titles.' Since then it is near-universally spoken of as a Dick Dale composition, when the melody was circulating among Arabic, Greek rebetiko and Jewish klezmer musicians by the 1920s and the earliest known recording is Demetriades's 1927 Columbia side. Dale himself said his arrangement came from hearing his uncle play the oud.
caveats: the folk melody's author 'is not known', yet Nicholas Roubanis, a Greek-American music instructor, credited himself as composer on a 1941 jazz instrumental arrangement, and because the claim was never legally challenged he 'is still officially credited as the composer today worldwide, except in Greece where credit is given to either Roubanis or Patrinos'. The earliest known recording is Theodotos Demetriades, 1927, Columbia — but the piece was already being played by Arabic, Greek rebetiko and Jewish klezmer musicians in the Ottoman Eastern Mediterranean by the 1920s, so even 1927 is 'earliest known', not 'first'.

songs.title: My Boy Lollipop
songs.writer: Robert Spencer of the Cadillacs (Morris Levy and Johnny Roberts listed themselves as the authors)
songs.whyNotable: The record that carried ska out of Jamaica and made Island Records a commercial concern is, in the popular account, where the song begins. It is not. Wikipedia records that Barbie Gaye recorded it first in 1956 on the Darl label, as a New York rock-and-roll side — eight years before Millie Small cut the ska version for Fontana/Island that reached number two in both the UK and the US, topped the Irish chart, sold over seven million copies and made Small an international star at sixteen. The credit history is as murky as the recording history: the song was written by Robert Spencer of the Cadillacs, but Morris Levy and Johnny Roberts listed themselves as the authors, and Levy went so far as to claim Spencer was a pseudonym of his own.
caveats: this is the earlier-recording case rather than a contested one, and it is the best find in the set. The recording almost universally called the original, Millie Small's 1964 ska hit, is a cover of Barbie Gaye's 1956 Darl single. Authorship is genuinely contested: Wikipedia states the song was written by Robert Spencer of the Cadillacs but that Morris Levy and Johnny Roberts listed themselves as authors, with Levy claiming Robert Spencer was a pseudonym of his own.

songs.title: Now That We Found Love
songs.whyNotable: Third World's 1978 reggae-disco reading on Island and Heavy D & the Boyz's 1991 hip-house one are the versions people know, and both are covers. Gamble and Huff wrote it for the O'Jays, who cut it at Sigma Sound for the 1973 album Ship Ahoy, where it was never a single.
caveats: 'the original' has two competing wrong answers depending on the listener's generation. Third World's 1978 Island version is taken as the original by UK and reggae listeners; Heavy D & the Boyz's 1991 version is taken as the original by a later audience that often assumes Third World's is itself the cover. The actual first recording, the O'Jays' 1973 Ship Ahoy track, is named by almost nobody. Whichever cover act the page leads with, the other should be addressed.

songs.title: Oh Carolina
songs.originalLabel: Wild Bells (Jamaica); licensed to Melodisc/Blue Beat in the UK
songs.writer: John Folkes (credit upheld in the UK High Court, 1994; the label had credited producer Prince Buster)
songs.whyNotable: Shaggy's 1993 breakthrough — two weeks at number one in the UK in March 1993, his first of four UK chart-toppers — is taken by most listeners as his own song. It is a cover of a Jamaican record more than thirty years older, produced by Prince Buster and sung by the Folkes Brothers. The authorship question is the page's real payload: because Jamaican singles of the period were routinely credited to the producer, Prince Buster's name sat on the label for decades and he maintained he had written it about a former girlfriend; John Folkes said he wrote it about his girlfriend, actually named Noelena, and the UK High Court upheld Folkes's claim in 1994, after Shaggy's hit had made the credit worth fighting over.
caveats: the two Wikipedia pages disagree on the date and do not reconcile. The song article says the Folkes Brothers recorded it in 1958 with the single released in 1960; the Prince Buster article says Buster produced it in 1961 on his Wild Bells label before it was licensed to Melodisc and issued on Blue Beat in the UK. I have used 1960 (the release year given on the song page) but this must be resolved against a discography before the record is written — this is exactly the Jamaican dating problem the vein warns about. Authorship is separately contested and resolved: the label credited producer Prince Buster, Buster claimed he wrote it, and John Folkes's claim was upheld in the UK High Court in 1994.

songs.title: One Step Beyond
songs.originalLabel: Blue Beat (UK outlet for Prince Buster's mid-60s ska)
songs.whyNotable: The song that named an era of British ska is, to almost everyone who owns the record, a Madness composition — it is the title track and opening cut of their 1979 debut on Stiff Records, released 19 October 1979 with the single following on 26 October. Wikipedia is explicit that Prince Buster recorded it first in 1964, as the B-side of 'Al Capone', and that his version was mostly instrumental apart from the title shouted a few times. Madness added the spoken Chas Smash intro and the chant, which is precisely why the cover reads as an original: the most quotable elements of the famous recording genuinely are Madness's, while the tune underneath is Buster's. The One Step Beyond... track listing credits it to Cecil Campbell, Buster's real name — a credit most listeners have never had a reason to read.

songs.title: One Way Out
songs.writer: Sonny Boy Williamson II (credits disputed; Elmore James may be a co-writer)
songs.whyNotable: A classic-rock radio staple universally filed under the Allman Brothers, who recorded it live at Fillmore East on 27 June 1971 and released it on Eat a Peach in 1972, with a single following in September 1972. Sonny Boy Williamson II recorded it in Chicago on 8 September 1961 and Chess's Checker label released it in January 1962 b/w "Nine Below Zero". The genuinely interesting wrinkle is that Elmore James cut a version with producer Bobby Robinson at Beltone Studios in late 1960 — earlier than Williamson's session — but it went unreleased until 1965, two years after James's death, on Sphere Sound. So first-recorded and first-released are different artists.
caveats: first-recorded and first-released are different artists. Elmore James recorded it with producer Bobby Robinson at Beltone Studios in late 1960 but it went unissued until 1965, after his death, on Sphere Sound; Sonny Boy Williamson II recorded 8 September 1961 and Checker released January 1962. Wikipedia calls it "a spontaneous composition by Williamson" while also noting commentary that the two, who performed together early on, may have been co-writers. The candidate above lists Williamson as originalArtist on first-release grounds; a page should carry the James session.

songs.title: Oye Como Va
songs.whyNotable: Wikipedia: "'Oye Cómo Va' is a 1962 cha-cha-chá song by Tito Puente, originally released on El Rey Bravo (Tico Records)." Santana recorded it for Abraxas in 1970 and took it to number 13 on the Hot 100 in 1971, and the Santana arrangement is now so dominant that the song is routinely assumed to be his. Puente wrote it and cut it eight years earlier as a mambo-band record, not a rock one.

songs.title: Reason to Believe
songs.whyNotable: Hardin wrote and recorded it in 1965; it was released on his debut Tim Hardin 1 on Verve in 1966. Stewart's version was issued as a single in July 1971 from Every Picture Tells a Story — famously as the A-side, with 'Maggie May' on the flip, until radio flipped it. Stewart returned to it on Unplugged...and Seated in 1993. The A-side history means Stewart's is the version people file the song under; Hardin, dead at 39, is a footnote to his own composition.

songs.title: Ruby, Don't Take Your Love to Town
songs.creditedTo: Kenny Rogers and the First Edition
songs.coverArtist: Kenny Rogers and the First Edition
songs.whyNotable: Tillis's song was first recorded by Waylon Jennings in 1966; the first commercial release was Johnny Darrell's 1967 United Artists single, which reached No. 9 country. Kenny Rogers and the First Edition recorded theirs in June 1968 and released it on Reprise in 1969, reaching No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 in the UK. The First Edition were a pop-rock act at the time, and their international hit erased both earlier country recordings from public memory.
caveats: Waylon Jennings recorded it first, in 1966, but the first COMMERCIAL release was Johnny Darrell's 1967 United Artists single (No. 9 country). First-recorded and first-released are different artists here.

songs.title: Scarborough Fair
songs.whyNotable: The ballad descends from the Scottish 'The Elfin Knight', documented as far back as 1670. The first commercial recording was by Gordon Heath and Lee Payant on the 1955 Elektra album Encores from the Abbaye. Martin Carthy recorded it on his 1965 debut, having learned it from the MacColl and Seeger songbook, and taught the arrangement to Paul Simon in London that year. Simon & Garfunkel released 'Scarborough Fair/Canticle' on Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme in 1966; the 1968 single reached No. 11. They credited only themselves, which caused a rift with Carthy until a 2000 duet — and the song is still widely assumed to be a Paul Simon composition.
caveats: first commercial recording is Gordon Heath and Lee Payant, 1955 (Elektra), but the version that matters causally is Martin Carthy's 1965 debut-album arrangement, which Paul Simon learned directly from Carthy in London and then copyrighted under his own name.

songs.title: Self Control
songs.writer: Giancarlo Bigazzi, Raffaele Riefoli (Raf) and Steve Piccolo
songs.whyNotable: The gap here is two months, not two decades, which is what makes it interesting: Wikipedia dates Raf's release to February 1984 on Carrere and Branigan's to 19 April 1984, and describes hers as a cover — "That same year, 'Self Control' was covered by American singer Laura Branigan." Branigan's went to number one in eight countries and number four in the US, which comprehensively buried the Italian original. Worth flagging on the page: Raf's original was itself sung in English, so the usual foreign-language tell is absent.

songs.title: Sing, Sing, Sing (With a Swing)
songs.originalArtist: Louis Prima and His New Orleans Gang
songs.whyNotable: This is the record that means "swing era" — Goodman's, with Gene Krupa's tom-toms, recorded in Hollywood on 6 July 1937 and immortalised at Carnegie Hall in 1938. Wikipedia is unambiguous about where it came from: "a 1936 song, with music and lyrics by Louis Prima, who first recorded it with his New Orleans Gang", released by Brunswick on 28 February 1936 with "It's Been So Long" as the B-side. Prima both wrote it and cut it first, roughly sixteen months ahead of Goodman.

songs.title: Sloop John B
songs.whyNotable: A Bahamian folk song from Nassau; a transcription was published by Richard Le Gallienne in Harper's Monthly in 1916 and Carl Sandburg included it in The American Songbag in 1927. The earliest recording listed by Wikipedia is The Weavers' in 1950, followed by The Kingston Trio (1958) — the version Al Jardine credits as the direct inspiration. The Beach Boys released their arrangement on 21 March 1966 as the second single from Pet Sounds, reaching No. 3 US and No. 2 UK. Sitting inside the most canonised album in pop, it is almost universally taken for a Brian Wilson original.
caveats: traditional Bahamian; the earliest recording listed by Wikipedia is The Weavers, 1950, but the song was in print by 1916 (Le Gallienne, Harper's Monthly) and 1927 (Sandburg, The American Songbag). 'The Weavers recorded it first' is the best available claim, not a confirmed one.

songs.title: Someday We'll Be Together
songs.writer: Johnny Bristol, Jackey Beavers and Harvey Fuqua
songs.whyNotable: The last of the Supremes' twelve American number ones was an eight-year-old record: Johnny Bristol and Jackey Beavers wrote it with Harvey Fuqua and cut it themselves as Johnny & Jackey for Tri-Phi in 1961. Bristol produced the 1969 Motown remake — on which, despite the credit, neither Mary Wilson nor Cindy Birdsong sang.

songs.title: Statesboro Blues
songs.whyNotable: For classic-rock listeners this is THE Allman Brothers song — Duane Allman's slide opening from At Fillmore East, which Rolling Stone ranked No. 9 on its 2008 "100 Greatest Guitar Songs of All Time". Blind Willie McTell wrote and recorded it on 17 October 1928 for Victor (Victor 38001), released January 1929, a forty-three year gap. The route was indirect: Taj Mahal's 1967 recording with Jesse Ed Davis on slide, issued on his 1968 debut, is what Duane heard — bandmate Pete Carr recalled that after seeing Taj Mahal perform it, "Duane started practicing slide all the time."
caveats: the Allman Brothers did not take it from Blind Willie McTell directly. Taj Mahal's 1967 recording with Jesse Ed Davis on slide, released on his 1968 debut, is the intermediary Duane Allman heard. A three-step chain, not two.

songs.title: Superstar
songs.originalArtist: Delaney and Bonnie and Friends featuring Eric Clapton
songs.whyNotable: The Carpenters' 1971 number 2 — later covered again by Luther Vandross and Sonic Youth — started life as a B-side. Delaney and Bonnie and Friends featuring Eric Clapton released it in December 1969 as the flip of 'Comin' Home', under the longer title 'Groupie (Superstar)'. Bonnie Bramlett co-wrote it with Leon Russell, from an idea by Rita Coolidge.
caveats: the Delaney & Bonnie first recording was issued in December 1969 under the title 'Groupie (Superstar)'; the shortened title arrived with later versions, and the Delaney & Bonnie recording itself was not put on an album until D&B Together in 1972.

songs.title: Suzie Q
songs.writer: Dale Hawkins, Robert Chaisson, Stan Lewis and Eleanor Broadwater
songs.whyNotable: CCR's first real hit and the track that broke them, so it reads as a CCR original — the eight-and-a-half-minute swamp-rock arrangement bears no obvious resemblance to a 1950s rockabilly single. Dale Hawkins recorded it at KWKH Radio in Shreveport and Checker released it in May 1957; it reached No. 7 R&B and No. 27 on the Hot 100. CCR's version was released 15 June 1968 and peaked at No. 11 in November 1968, split across the A and B sides to get airplay. Hawkins co-wrote it with bandmate Robert Chaisson, though Stan Lewis and Eleanor Broadwater took credits to share royalties.

songs.title: Those Were the Days
songs.originalArtist: The Limeliters (first English-language recording); the underlying Russian romance is "Dorogoi dlinnoyu" by Boris Fomin
songs.writer: Boris Fomin (music) and Konstantin Podrevsky (Russian lyrics); English lyrics by Gene Raskin
songs.whyNotable: Apple Records' second-ever single, produced by Paul McCartney, a UK and Canadian number one — it presents as a Mary Hopkin original and is filed that way in most people's heads. It is a Russian romance, "Dorogoi dlinnoyu", composed by Boris Fomin to a Podrevsky lyric; Gene Raskin wrote the English words, and per Wikipedia "The Limeliters subsequently released a recording of the song on its 1962 LP Folk Matinee" — six years before Hopkin.

songs.title: Universal Soldier
songs.whyNotable: Sainte-Marie wrote it in a Toronto coffee-house basement and released her own recording on her Vanguard debut It's My Way! in April 1964. Donovan cut it for the UK EP The Universal Soldier (15 August 1965); Hickory issued it as a US single in September 1965, reaching No. 53. Glen Campbell also charted a version in 1965 (No. 45 US). Donovan's is the version anthologised in every sixties protest compilation, and the song is habitually filed under his name rather than Sainte-Marie's.
caveats: Buffy Sainte-Marie's own recording (It's My Way!, Vanguard, April 1964) was NOT the first release: the folk group The Highwaymen issued it as a single in September 1963. The candidate names Sainte-Marie as originalArtist because she wrote it and her recording is the one Donovan's descends from, but a page on this song should lead with the Highwaymen single.

songs.title: Where Did You Sleep Last Night
songs.whyNotable: Known traditionally as 'In the Pines', the song grew out of two anonymous Southern Appalachian songs dating to at least the 1870s; commercial recordings begin in 1926, and Judith McCulloh's 1970 dissertation identified 160 variants. Lead Belly recorded several versions in the 1940s, and his 1944 Musicraft recording is the one Cobain's reading follows in form and title. Nirvana performed it at MTV Unplugged on 18 November 1993; it was released posthumously in November 1994 as the closing track of MTV Unplugged in New York. Kurt Cobain named Lead Belly on stage, yet a generation still hears it as a Nirvana song.
caveats: Lead Belly is NOT the first recorder. Wikipedia states commercial recordings begin in 1926 and that the song derives from two anonymous Appalachian songs dating to at least the 1870s; McCulloh counted 160 variants. Lead Belly's 1944 Musicraft version is only the proximate source for Nirvana. Do not assert a first recording for this one.

songs.title: Wild Thing
songs.whyNotable: One of the most recognisable records of the British Invasion and taken as a Troggs original by essentially everyone. In fact a New York band called The Wild Ones cut the first studio version, released November 1965, which flopped. The Troggs released theirs on 22 April 1966 on Fontana (issued in the US on both Fontana and Atco because of a distribution dispute), and it topped the Billboard Hot 100 on 30 July 1966 and reached No. 2 in the UK. Chip Taylor wrote it.

songs.title: Woo-Hoo
songs.whyNotable: Universally known as 'the Kill Bill song' and filed under a Japanese all-female garage trio, it is a 1959 Virginia rockabilly instrumental. George Donald McGraw wrote it and released it with The Rock-A-Teens in September 1959 on Roulette; the credit had originally sat with Dick Moran and Doran Records before McGraw bought and renamed it. The 5.6.7.8's recorded their version for the 1996 album Bomb the Twist, where it stayed obscure in the West until they performed it on screen in Kill Bill: Volume 1 (2003). A Carling beer advert followed, and the cover reached No. 28 on the UK Singles Chart in 2004 — a rare Western chart placing for a Japanese band — plus a US Vonage campaign. Because the track is essentially wordless beyond the title, nothing in it signals its age or origin.

songs.title: You're My World
songs.writer: Umberto Bindi and Gino Paoli; English lyrics by Carl Sigman
songs.whyNotable: A UK number one for four weeks from the chart dated 30 May 1964, on Parlophone, recorded at Abbey Road on 3 April 1964 — about as British-Invasion a provenance as a record can have. It is an Italian song: "Il mio mondo", written and first recorded by Umberto Bindi with Gino Paoli in 1963. Wikipedia notes the original "was not a hit, even in Italy" before it reached George Martin, which is exactly why nobody suspects it exists.

songs.title: You're Wondering Now
songs.writer: Clement Seymour Dodd (credited on The Specials' album; some sources credit Rueben Anderson)
songs.whyNotable: The closing track of The Specials' 1979 debut on 2 Tone reads as the band's own sign-off — a valedictory written for the end of a record — and Amy Winehouse's later performances of it reinforced the association with British rather than Jamaican music. Wikipedia's entry on the album states plainly that it was originally performed by Andy & Joey in 1964, and later covered by the Skatalites. Andy & Joey are about as obscure as a source act gets, which is exactly the condition under which a cover quietly becomes an original in public memory.
caveats: the writer credit conflicts across sources. The Wikipedia article on The Specials' debut album credits 'Clement Seymour' (i.e. Clement Seymour Dodd, of Studio One); non-Wikipedia sources encountered in search, which I did not treat as verified, credit Rueben Anderson, who was himself the 'Andy' of Andy & Joey. Producer-as-credited-writer was standard Jamaican practice at the time, so this may be the same pattern as Oh Carolina. The 1964 Andy & Joey original recording is not in doubt; only the authorship is. I could not find a standalone Wikipedia article for the song, and no label is asserted here because none appears on a page I fetched.

songs.title: You've Made Me So Very Happy
songs.writer: Brenda Holloway, Patrice Holloway, Frank Wilson and Berry Gordy Jr.
songs.whyNotable: Blood, Sweat & Tears took it to number 2 in April 1969, held off the top only by 'Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In'. Brenda Holloway had released it on Tamla on August 17, 1967 — and co-wrote it, with her sister Patrice, Frank Wilson and Berry Gordy. It is the rare Motown record so thoroughly outsold by its cover that the original effectively disappeared.

songs.title: Baby, Come Back
songs.whyNotable: Pato Banton's version, released 19 September 1994 with Robin and Ali Campbell of UB40 guesting, went to number one in the UK and finished as the fourth-biggest-selling single of that year — a scale of success that tends to erase what came before it. The Equals recorded it first, released 9 June 1967 on President Records as a B-side, and it went to number one in the UK, Belgium and Rhodesia across 1967 and 1968. The writer is Eddy Grant, the Equals' guitarist, well before his solo career; listeners who know Grant as a solo name and Banton as a reggae name rarely connect either to a 1967 beat-group B-side.

songs.title: Baltimore
songs.whyNotable: Nina Simone's reggae reading is the version that survives, and it is generally heard as hers — a piece of first-person testimony about an American city. It is a Randy Newman song, written and first recorded for his 1977 album Little Criminals and issued as a single on Warner Bros. in 1978; Simone's cover became the title track of her own 1978 album Baltimore, recast as reggae. Newman has said the lyric came from a National Geographic article rather than firsthand knowledge — he remarked that a lot of his songs are about places he has never been or does not know well — which sits oddly against the authority Simone's delivery lends it. The Jamaican trio the Tamlins cut their own reggae version in 1979.

songs.title: Cherry Oh Baby
songs.whyNotable: Eric Donaldson wrote and recorded this in 1971 and won that year's Jamaica Song Festival with it — in Jamaica it is a standard, and Donaldson is the answer. Outside Jamaica the answer is usually UB40, whose version was released 27 February 1984 as the fourth single from Labour of Love, reaching number 12 in the UK, number seven in both Ireland and the Netherlands, and number one in Paraguay, with silver certification in the UK and platinum in New Zealand. The Rolling Stones had recorded it for Black and Blue in 1976, a version that never achieved the same recognition, so even the cover most rock listeners might know is not the one that shaped the misattribution.

songs.title: Crossroads
songs.whyNotable: Cream's "Crossroads" is one of the most celebrated guitar performances in rock and is habitually discussed as Clapton's own showpiece rather than as a Robert Johnson record — helped by the title change, since Johnson's is "Cross Road Blues". Johnson recorded it on 27 November 1936 at the Gunter Hotel in San Antonio and Vocalion released it in May 1937 b/w "Ramblin' on My Mind". Cream's version was taped live at the Winterland Ballroom on 10 March 1968, issued on Wheels of Fire and released as an Atco single in January 1969, reaching No. 28 on the Hot 100. Clapton had already cut a version in early 1966 with the ad hoc Eric Clapton and the Powerhouse, while in John Mayall's Bluesbreakers.
caveats: the title differs from the original. Robert Johnson recorded "Cross Road Blues" (27 November 1936, Vocalion, released May 1937); Cream's is "Crossroads". Clapton had also recorded it in early 1966 with the one-off Eric Clapton and the Powerhouse, before the 10 March 1968 Winterland live take that became the famous record.

songs.title: Der Kommissar
songs.whyNotable: In the US this is an After the Fire record: their English-language version, released 28 May 1982 on Epic, reached number five on the Hot 100 in 1983 on the back of MTV, while Falco's own original stalled at number 74 on the Cash Box chart. Wikipedia records the German original as a 1981 Falco recording written with producer Robert Ponger, released on GiG and A&M, and a number one in Austria, Italy, Spain and West Germany. Rated medium rather than high only because Falco later became famous in America on his own account.

songs.title: I Can't Quit You Baby
songs.whyNotable: Otis Rush is not a name the general listener knows, so the Led Zeppelin I track tends to be heard as Zeppelin's own slow blues, in a catalogue notorious for uncredited borrowing. Rush's version was the first recording, cut in 1956 and released on Cobra in August 1956, reaching No. 6 on Billboard's R&B chart; it entered the Blues Foundation Hall of Fame in 1994. Willie Dixon wrote it. The specific detail that makes the page: Cub Koda describes Zeppelin's reading as a note-for-note copy not of the 1956 Cobra single but of Rush's later 1966 Vanguard recording. Over thirty artists have recorded it.

songs.title: I Say a Little Prayer
songs.whyNotable: One of the most frequently corrected attributions in soul. Aretha's Atlantic single, released July 26, 1968, came out of the group larking about with the song in rehearsal, and it reached number 10. Dionne Warwick had recorded Bacharach and David's original at a session on April 9, 1966, though Scepter held it back until the autumn of 1967.
caveats: Dionne Warwick recorded it on April 9, 1966 but Scepter held it until it appeared on The Windows of the World in September 1967 and as a single in October 1967. originalYear above is the RECORDING year, per the locked definition; a release-year page would say 1967.

songs.title: Knock on Wood
songs.whyNotable: Amii Stewart's version topped the Hot 100 in April 1979 and reads to a lot of listeners as a purpose-built disco record. Eddie Floyd wrote it with Steve Cropper and cut it at Stax on July 13, 1966, released twelve days later. David Bowie also charted a live version at number 10 in the UK in 1974.

songs.title: Lady Marmalade
songs.creditedTo: Christina Aguilera, Lil' Kim, Mýa and Pink
songs.coverArtist: Christina Aguilera, Lil' Kim, Mýa and Pink
songs.whyNotable: For anyone who was a teenager in 2001, this is a Christina Aguilera record. It was made for Moulin Rouge!, released 10 April 2001 on Interscope, produced by Missy Elliott and Rockwilder, and it spent five weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100, took the 2002 Grammy for Best Pop Collaboration with Vocals and the 2001 MTV Video of the Year. Labelle's original, written by Bob Crewe and Kenny Nolan, was cut at Sea-Saint Studios in New Orleans with Allen Toussaint producing, released 5 November 1974 on Epic, and spent a week at No. 1 on 29 March 1975. Rated medium rather than high because Labelle's version was itself a chart-topper and remains in circulation — but the film soundtrack is squarely what re-anchored the song to four singers who were not born when it was written. See contested: there is an earlier recording still.
caveats: Wikipedia states that before Labelle's version a demo was recorded by The Eleventh Hour, a disco group fronted by co-writer Kenny Nolan on vocals, appearing on the 1974 album Eleventh Hour's Greatest Hits, which did not chart. Both that album and Labelle's 5 November 1974 Epic single are dated 1974, so the ordering rests entirely on Wikipedia's wording ('before Labelle's famous version') and not on two dated sources I could compare. If this record is built, the honest framing is a three-step chain — Eleventh Hour demo, Labelle hit, Moulin Rouge! remake — with the first step flagged as unconfirmed in month order.

songs.title: Police and Thieves
songs.whyNotable: The unusual fact here is the chart sequence, which is documented and runs the wrong way. Junior Murvin brought the song to Lee 'Scratch' Perry at Black Ark in May 1976 and Perry recorded it the same afternoon, altering the lyrics slightly. The Clash recorded their version in March 1977 for a debut album released 8 April 1977, after Strummer and Simonon encountered the record at the 1976 Notting Hill Carnival. Murvin's original did not reach the UK Singles Chart until 1980, peaking at number 23 after being used in the film Rockers — three years after the cover had already put the song in front of a British rock audience, which is precisely the condition under which a cover gets mistaken for a source.

songs.title: Rock Island Line
songs.originalLabel: Library of Congress field recording (John A. Lomax)
songs.whyNotable: The first audio recording was made by John A. Lomax on 29 September 1934 at the Tucker prison farm in Arkansas, usually identified as Kelly Pace and prisoners. Lead Belly first recorded his own narrative version on 22 June 1937 in Washington, D.C. Donegan recorded his up-tempo reading in July 1954 and released it as a single in late 1955; it reached No. 8 in the US and was the first debut record certified gold in the UK, triggering the skiffle craze. In Britain the song is filed as Donegan's; among American listeners who know better, Lead Belly is usually named as the original — and he was not the first either.
caveats: same shape. Lead Belly (22 June 1937) is the standard 'original' answer, but Lomax's 29 September 1934 Tucker prison-farm recording, credited to Kelly Pace and prisoners, predates it.

songs.title: Sitting on Top of the World
songs.whyNotable: The song has been absorbed so completely into so many traditions that almost nobody points at the right origin: rock listeners assign it to Cream's slow Wheels of Fire version (1968), blues listeners to Howlin' Wolf's 1957 Chicago-blues rework, which he often used to close his sets, and country and bluegrass audiences to Milton Brown, Bob Wills or Bill Monroe. It was first recorded in 1930 by the Mississippi Sheiks for Okeh, written by group members Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon — Vinson said he composed it one morning after playing a dance in Greenwood, Mississippi. The Grateful Dead played it at 252 bpm; Cream played it at 44.
caveats: the usual answer is Howlin' Wolf (1957), which is itself a cover. The first recording is the Mississippi Sheiks, 1930 on Okeh, written by Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon. It is simultaneously claimed by blues, country and bluegrass traditions.

songs.title: Softly, as I Leave You
songs.writer: Tony De Vita (music) and Giorgio Calabrese (Italian lyrics); English lyrics by Hal Shaper
songs.whyNotable: Sinatra gave it his 1964 album title and it sits in his catalogue as a Sinatra song (number 27 Hot 100, number four Easy Listening). It is Italian: "Piano", by Tony De Vita and Giorgio Calabrese, and per Wikipedia "Mina published a recording of the song first as a single in 1960". Hal Shaper wrote the English words in November 1961. Two removes from Sinatra, not one — see contested.
caveats: there are two claimants ahead of Sinatra, not one. Mina's Italian "Piano" single (1960) is the original recording, but Matt Monro recorded the first English-language version in 1962 on Parlophone, two years before Sinatra's 1964 album. British listeners often credit Monro and Americans credit Sinatra; both are covering Mina.

songs.title: Way Down in the Hole
songs.whyNotable: Tom Waits wrote it and first recorded it in 1987 on Franks Wild Years. The version most people have heard is the Blind Boys of Alabama gospel reading that opened the first season of The Wire, which premiered on HBO on 2 June 2002 — and the natural assumption is that a Blind Boys of Alabama gospel number is an old spiritual the show licensed, not a Tom Waits song from a 1987 art-rock album. The series then cycled the song through a different artist each season (the Blind Boys of Alabama, Waits himself, The Neville Brothers, DoMaJe and Steve Earle), which further detaches it from any single 'original' in a viewer's mind; an extended cut of the Blind Boys recording plays over a montage in the series finale. Rated medium: the misattribution is real but softer than the others here, since season two returns the Waits recording to the credits.
caveats: I could confirm that the Blind Boys of Alabama recorded the season one version and that The Wire premiered on 2 June 2002, but I could NOT verify the date on which their recording was made (the Wikipedia URL I tried for the album resolved to an unrelated role-playing game). The coverYear of 2002 is therefore the year the version reached the public as the theme, not a verified recording date. Confirm before the page asserts a recording year.

songs.title: You Shook Me
songs.whyNotable: Sits on Led Zeppelin I next to several other borrowed blues and is generally taken as Zeppelin's. Muddy Waters's Chess single was released in 1962; Willie Dixon and J.B. Lenoir wrote it, with Dixon supplying the lyrics. The story is unusually tangled even for this vein: the backing track began as Earl Hooker's instrumental "Blue Guitar", from a 1961 session, released on Age Records in 1962 — Leonard Chess acquired it and had Waters overdub vocals on 27 June 1962. And the more immediate dispute is not with the bluesman but with a peer: the Jeff Beck Group released theirs on 29 July 1968, Zeppelin recorded on 27 September 1968 and released on 12 January 1969. Page denied hearing Beck's, but biographers note he attended Jeff Beck Group shows on their 1968 US tour, that Peter Grant had an advance copy of Truth, and that John Paul Jones played organ on both records.
caveats: the record credited to Muddy Waters (Chess, 1962) is built on Earl Hooker's instrumental, cut at a 1961 session as "Blue Guitar" and released on Age Records in 1962. Leonard Chess acquired the track and had Waters overdub vocals on 27 June 1962. So the first recording of the music is Hooker's, and the Muddy Waters "original" is an overdub onto someone else's master.

songs.title: Young, Gifted and Black
songs.whyNotable: In Britain this is a reggae record: Bob and Marcia's version reached number five on the UK Singles Chart in 1970 and number 15 in Ireland, and for a large part of the UK audience that is where the song starts. Nina Simone wrote the music to Weldon Irvine's lyrics, taking the title from Lorraine Hansberry's To Be Young, Gifted and Black; she recorded it at Philharmonic Hall on 26 October 1969 for the live album Black Gold, issued by RCA in 1970. The two versions landed within months of each other, which is part of why the Jamaican one was able to take root in the UK as the definitive reading rather than as a cover. Aretha Franklin's version followed on her 1972 album of the same name.
caveats: the two versions are both dated 1970 and the title differs between them (Nina Simone's is 'To Be Young, Gifted and Black'; Bob and Marcia's is 'Young, Gifted and Black'). Simone's precedence rests on the recording date of 26 October 1969 at Philharmonic Hall rather than on a release-year gap, and the Bob and Marcia single is dated only to 1970 on the page I fetched. Do not state an interval between the two — no month is documented for the cover.

songs.title: Zou Bisou Bisou
songs.writer: Bill Shepherd and Alan Tew, with French lyrics by Michel Rivgauche
songs.whyNotable: A song that arrived in the Anglophone world so completely attached to one television scene that most viewers assumed it was written for the show. It is a genuine 1960 yé-yé record: Gillian Hills released the first version as her debut single that summer, composed by Bill Shepherd and Alan Tew with French lyrics by Michel Rivgauche, and George Martin produced an English adaptation, 'Zoo Be Zoo Be Zoo', for Sophia Loren in The Millionairess. Jessica Paré performed it as Megan Draper at Don's fortieth birthday party in the Mad Men season five premiere, 'A Little Kiss'. It trended on Twitter, drew write-ups in Rolling Stone, The Wall Street Journal and Slate, was parodied by The Roots on Late Night with Jimmy Fallon the following night, and eventually charted at No. 100 on the Canadian Hot 100 on 14 April 2012. Medium rather than high because the confusion runs 'written for the show' rather than naming a rival artist.

songs.title: A Message to You, Rudy
songs.whyNotable: The 2 Tone anthem is assumed to be a Specials original, but Dandy Livingstone wrote and recorded it in London in 1967; Rico Rodriguez played the trombone intro on both his version and the Specials' 1979 remake.

songs.title: Babe I'm Gonna Leave You
songs.whyNotable: Written by Anne Bredon in the late 1950s; the first published recording was Joan Baez's 1962 in-concert album, credited there only as traditional. Zeppelin's 1969 debut credited it 'Traditional, arr. Jimmy Page' until Bredon approached the band and won credit plus back royalties in 1990.

songs.title: Beyond the Sea
songs.writer: Charles Trenet (French original 'La Mer'); Jack Lawrence (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: Trenet's 'La Mer' was published in 1946, but the first recording was made by Roland Gerbeau in December 1945, ahead of Trenet's own. Jack Lawrence's English lyric turned an ode to the sea into a love song; Darin's Atco single did not appear until January 1960.

songs.title: Black Magic Woman
songs.whyNotable: Peter Green wrote and recorded it for early Fleetwood Mac in 1968; Santana's 1970 version is the one everyone thinks is original.

songs.title: Blinded by the Light
songs.whyNotable: Manfred Mann's Earth Band took it to No. 1 (1977); it's remembered as theirs, not Springsteen's 1973 original.

songs.title: Blue Suede Shoes
songs.whyNotable: Carl Perkins wrote AND first recorded it; Elvis's fame led the public to assume it was his.

songs.title: Bring It On Home
songs.whyNotable: Recorded by Sonny Boy Williamson II on 11 January 1963 for Checker and released in 1966. Zeppelin's Led Zeppelin II track opened and closed with deliberate quotations of it; Chess publisher Arc Music sued, the band settled, and later reissues give Willie Dixon sole songwriting credit.

songs.title: Cry Baby
songs.whyNotable: Garnet Mimms took it to No. 1 R&B and No. 4 pop in 1963, but Joplin's posthumous Pearl version is so identified with her that Mimms has largely vanished from the song's story.

songs.title: Dazed and Confused
songs.whyNotable: Holmes wrote and recorded it for his 1967 debut album; Led Zeppelin's 1969 debut credited it to Jimmy Page alone. Holmes sued Page in 2010, the case was dismissed with prejudice in January 2012 after a settlement, and later releases changed the credit to 'By Page - Inspired by Jake Holmes'.

songs.title: Delta Dawn
songs.whyNotable: Co-writer Alex Harvey recorded it first, on his November 1971 Capitol album; Tanya Tucker's April 1972 Columbia country hit came next, and Helen Reddy's June 1973 pop version - a US No. 1 - is the one most people name.

songs.title: Don't Turn Around
songs.whyNotable: Twice mistaken: Ace of Base's 1994 hit is usually taken as theirs, and those who know better usually credit Aswad's 1988 UK No. 1 reggae version - but the first recording was Tina Turner's, issued in 1986 as the B-side of 'Typical Male'.

songs.title: Everybody Needs Somebody to Love
songs.writer: Bert Berns, Solomon Burke and Jerry Wexler
songs.whyNotable: Solomon Burke co-wrote and recorded it on 28 May 1964, released that July on Atlantic; the 1980 Blues Brothers film performance is now the default reference point for a whole generation. The Rolling Stones had already covered it in January 1965.

songs.title: Everybody's Talkin'
songs.whyNotable: The textbook sync case: Nilsson's 1968 recording flopped as a single, then Midnight Cowboy made it a hit so total that the song is now subtitled 'Theme from Midnight Cowboy'. Fred Neil wrote and recorded it first, on his self-titled Capitol album released December 1966.

songs.title: Fly Me to the Moon
songs.whyNotable: Bart Howard wrote it in 1954 as 'In Other Words', and the first commercial recording was Kaye Ballard's, issued by Decca in April 1954 and reviewed in Billboard that May. Sinatra's Count Basie/Quincy Jones recording came a decade later, in 1964, and swallowed the song's identity whole.

songs.title: Girl You Know It's True
songs.whyNotable: Written and first recorded by the little-known Maryland group Numarx earlier the same year Milli Vanilli's global hit landed.

songs.title: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
songs.whyNotable: Robert Hazard wrote and demoed it in 1979 as a male-perspective song; almost no one knows a man recorded it first.

songs.title: Hooked on a Feeling
songs.whyNotable: B. J. Thomas recorded it first, released October 1968 on Scepter. Blue Swede's 1974 cover bolted on a chanted intro borrowed from a 1971 Jonathan King version, and Reservoir Dogs plus the Guardians of the Galaxy trailers made that arrangement the only one most listeners have ever heard.

songs.title: Hound Dog
songs.whyNotable: Elvis's 1956 smash so dominated memory that most never encounter Big Mama Thornton's 1952 R&B original.

songs.title: Hurt
songs.whyNotable: Reznor wrote and recorded it for NIN (1994); Cash's 2003 version is so definitive Reznor said 'that song isn't mine anymore.'

songs.title: I Can See Clearly Now
songs.whyNotable: The reverse-direction trap: because Jimmy Cliff's Cool Runnings version is the one a generation grew up with, the song is often taken for a Jamaican reggae standard, when it was written and recorded by American singer Johnny Nash and was a US No. 1 in 1972.

songs.title: I Love Rock 'n' Roll
songs.whyNotable: British band Arrows recorded it first (1975); Jett's 1982 chart-topper is assumed to be the source.

songs.title: If You Don't Know Me by Now
songs.whyNotable: A Philly soul landmark sung by Teddy Pendergrass (No. 1 R&B, No. 3 pop, 1972) that a generation now hears as a Simply Red song after Mick Hucknall's 1989 US No. 1. Gamble and Huff originally wrote it for Labelle, who never recorded it.

songs.title: It's All Over Now
songs.whyNotable: Bobby Womack's group the Valentinos recorded it on 24 March 1964 for Sam Cooke's SAR label and reached only No. 94; the Stones cut theirs at Chess Studios on 10 June, releasing it on 26 June for their first UK No. 1. Barely three months separate the original from the version that erased it.

songs.title: Kingston Town
songs.whyNotable: UB40's signature ballad, a UK No. 4 and a No. 1 in France and the Netherlands, is a cover of Lord Creator's 1970 Clandisc single produced by Clancy Eccles - the same Labour of Love covers-project trap as their Red Red Wine.

songs.title: Land of 1000 Dances
songs.whyNotable: New Orleans R&B singer Chris Kenner wrote and first recorded it on Instant in 1962; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic cut (No. 6 pop, No. 1 R&B) is the best-known version and is widely assumed to be the original. The famous chanted hook belongs to neither - Cannibal & the Headhunters added it on their 1965 Rampart version.

songs.title: Louie Louie
songs.whyNotable: The Kingsmen's 1963 garage-rock hit buried Richard Berry's 1957 original, a B-side he wrote and first recorded.

songs.title: Love Hurts
songs.whyNotable: The Everly Brothers cut it first in July 1960 and buried it as an album track on A Date with the Everly Brothers - never a single. Nazareth's 1974 power-ballad rendition is the only version ever to be a US hit single, which is why the song reads as a Scottish hard-rock original.

songs.title: Make You Feel My Love
songs.whyNotable: Bob Dylan wrote it, but Billy Joel's recording (as 'To Make You Feel My Love', 13 August 1997) reached the public first, ahead of Dylan's own Time Out of Mind release on 30 September 1997. Adele's 2008 version, propelled by X Factor performances in 2010, is now widely assumed to be the song's origin.

songs.title: Me and Bobby McGee
songs.whyNotable: Joplin's posthumous 1971 No. 1 is so hers that few know Roger Miller recorded it first in 1969.

songs.title: Mustang Sally
songs.whyNotable: Mack Rice wrote it and cut it himself as 'Sir Mack Rice' for Blue Rock in May 1965; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic version buried it so completely that the song is now treated as a Pickett original.

songs.title: My Way
songs.writer: Jacques Revaux (music); Claude François and Gilles Thibaut (original French lyrics); Paul Anka (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The definitive Sinatra signature song is an English rewrite of the French chanson 'Comme d'habitude', recorded and released by Claude François in November 1967. Paul Anka bought the adaptation rights after hearing the tune on French radio.

songs.title: Nothing Compares 2 U
songs.whyNotable: Prince wrote it and his side project The Family recorded it first (1985, no single); O'Connor's 1990 hit is taken as the original.

songs.title: Papa Was a Rollin' Stone
songs.whyNotable: Whitfield gave it to the Undisputed Truth first - single released 9 May 1972 on Gordy, a modest No. 63 pop - then re-cut it with the Temptations four months later for a Hot 100 No. 1 and three Grammys. Same label, same producer, and the first version is almost entirely forgotten.

songs.title: Pass the Dutchie
songs.writer: The Mighty Diamonds (adapted from Leroy Sibbles' 1968 instrumental 'Full Up')
songs.whyNotable: Musical Youth's 1982 UK No. 1 is remembered as a novelty original, but it is a sanitised retitling of The Mighty Diamonds' 1981 'Pass the Kouchie'; a 2012 High Court case confirmed the two share the same copyright.

songs.title: Piece of My Heart
songs.whyNotable: Joplin's 1968 Big Brother version buried Erma Franklin's 1967 soul original.

songs.title: Red Red Wine
songs.whyNotable: UB40 themselves didn't know Neil Diamond wrote it (1967); their 1983 reggae version is taken as the original.

songs.title: Respect
songs.whyNotable: Aretha's 1967 reworking became so definitive the public rarely knows Otis Redding wrote and first recorded it in 1965.

songs.title: Rhinestone Cowboy
songs.whyNotable: Writer Larry Weiss recorded it himself on his 1974 album Black and Blue Suite, where it made no commercial impact outside a No. 71 placing in Australia; Campbell's May 1975 version topped both the Hot 100 and the country chart and became his signature song.

songs.title: Rivers of Babylon
songs.whyNotable: One of the best-selling UK singles ever and universally filed as Euro-disco by Boney M., yet it was written and recorded in 1970 by Jamaican rocksteady group The Melodians for Leslie Kong, and reached the world via The Harder They Come.

songs.title: Seasons in the Sun
songs.whyNotable: Brel recorded the French original 'Le Moribond' on 22 February 1961, released that July. The Kingston Trio cut the first English version in 1963 using Rod McKuen's adaptation; Terry Jacks recorded his own reworking in Vancouver in 1973.

songs.title: Seven Bridges Road
songs.whyNotable: Country-folk songwriter Steve Young wrote and first recorded it for his 1969 A&M album Rock Salt & Nails; the Eagles' harmony live version, recorded 28 July 1980 and issued as a single that December, reached No. 21 and is now assumed to be an Eagles original.

songs.title: Some Kind of Wonderful
songs.whyNotable: John Ellison wrote it and cut it with his own R&B group Soul Brothers Six for Atlantic in 1967, where it stalled at No. 91. Grand Funk's December 1974 Capitol single hit No. 3, and the song is now heard as a rock original rather than a failed soul 45.

songs.title: Sukiyaki
songs.whyNotable: Released in Japan on 15 October 1961 as 'Ue o Muite Arukō', Kyu Sakamoto's record was renamed 'Sukiyaki' abroad. A Taste of Honey's 1981 version used entirely new English words, and 4 P.M.'s 1994 hit copied that arrangement, leaving two generations who never met the Japanese original.

songs.title: Suspicious Minds
songs.whyNotable: Mark James's 1968 original flopped uncharted; Elvis's 1969 comeback smash is universally taken as the original.

songs.title: Sway
songs.originalArtist: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
songs.writer: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz (original); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The Mexican bolero-mambo '¿Quién será?' was first recorded as an instrumental by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta for RCA Victor in 1953. Dean Martin's Capitol single of 1954 carried Norman Gimbel's unrelated English lyric, and Michael Bublé's 2004 revival pushed the Spanish original further out of view.

songs.title: Tennessee Waltz
songs.originalArtist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
songs.writer: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
songs.whyNotable: Pee Wee King's band recorded it 2 December 1947 and RCA Victor released it in January 1948, a No. 3 country hit; Patti Page's November 1950 Mercury pop version spent nine weeks at No. 1 and eclipsed the country original entirely.

songs.title: The Best
songs.whyNotable: Bonnie Tyler released it first, in January 1988 from her album Hide Your Heart. Tina Turner's August 1989 Capitol cover - which added a bridge and a key change at her request - became the version used across decades of advertising and is near-universally taken for the original.

songs.title: The First Cut Is the Deepest
songs.whyNotable: Soul singer P. P. Arnold released the first recording on 21 April 1967 on Immediate, months before writer Cat Stevens issued his own version on New Masters (15 December 1967). Rod Stewart's 1977 hit and Sheryl Crow's 2003 version are what most listeners know, and the song's first voice was neither.

songs.title: The Girl from Ipanema
songs.writer: Antônio Carlos Jobim (music); Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: 'Garota de Ipanema' was written in 1962 and first commercially recorded that year by Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro. The Getz/Gilberto recording everyone treats as the original was taped in March 1963 and released on Verve in March 1964.

songs.title: The House of the Rising Sun
songs.whyNotable: The oldest known recording is the Appalachian duo Ashley and Foster's, cut 6 September 1933 for Vocalion. Guthrie, Lead Belly, Josh White, Baez, Simone and Dylan all recorded it before the Animals' June 1964 single, which the public treats as the song's point of origin.

songs.title: The Lion Sleeps Tonight
songs.writer: Solomon Linda (original); George David Weiss (English adaptation)
songs.whyNotable: The a cappella Zulu record 'Mbube' was cut by Solomon Linda's group at Gallo's Johannesburg studio in 1939. It reached the West via Alan Lomax and The Weavers' 'Wimoweh' (1951) before The Tokens' RCA Victor single of October 1961 became the version the world credits - while Linda received essentially nothing.

songs.title: The Tide Is High
