songs.whyNotable: Blondie's 1980 US and UK No. 1 is routinely treated as a Blondie song, but it is a cover of a 1967 Jamaican rocksteady single by The Paragons, written by their lead singer John Holt and cut for Duke Reid's Treasure Isle.

songs.title: The Train Kept A-Rollin'
songs.writer: Tiny Bradshaw, Lois Mann and Howard Kay
songs.whyNotable: A classic-rock staple most listeners file under Aerosmith began as a jump-blues record cut by bandleader Tiny Bradshaw in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951. 'Lois Mann' is a pseudonym of King Records owner Syd Nathan, added so the label boss could collect publishing royalties.

songs.title: Time Is on My Side
songs.writer: Jerry Ragovoy (as 'Norman Meade'), with lyrics by Jimmy Norman
songs.whyNotable: The Stones' first US top ten is a cover twice over: Irma Thomas cut it in April 1964, but the first recording was jazz trombonist Kai Winding's, released on Verve in October 1963. The verse lyrics everyone knows were written by session singer Jimmy Norman at the Thomas session.

songs.title: Torn
songs.writer: Scott Cutler, Anne Preven, Phil Thornalley
songs.whyNotable: Written 1991; first RELEASED as the Danish 'Brændt' by Lis Sørensen (1993), then in English by Ednaswap (1995); Imbruglia's 1997 hit is assumed original — many think she wrote it.

songs.title: Try a Little Tenderness
songs.originalArtist: Ray Noble Orchestra (vocal by Val Rosing)
songs.writer: Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly
songs.whyNotable: Published November 1932 and first recorded that December by the Ray Noble Orchestra. Otis Redding's 1966 Volt/Atco reading is so definitive that almost nobody knows it is a cover of a pre-war standard.

songs.title: Twist and Shout
songs.whyNotable: The Beatles' 1963 recording is so theirs that few know the Top Notes cut it first in 1961 (the Isley Brothers 1962 is also earlier).

songs.title: Unchained Melody
songs.whyNotable: Written for the 1955 prison film Unchained and first recorded by Todd Duncan for that film. The Righteous Brothers cut their version in March 1965 for Philles, originally a B-side, and the 1990 film Ghost made that recording the version an entire generation met first - and assumes is the original.

songs.title: Valerie
songs.whyNotable: The 2007 Ronson/Winehouse soul version so eclipsed the Liverpool indie band's 2006 original that most assume it's a Winehouse song.

songs.title: Wagon Wheel
songs.whyNotable: Old Crow Medicine Show's string-band version, released 10 February 2004, spread by word of mouth and never charted mainstream; Rucker's 2013 Capitol single hit No. 1 country and went 11x platinum. The chorus itself is an unfinished 1973 Dylan sketch that Secor built verses around.

songs.title: War
songs.whyNotable: The Temptations recorded it first, on the March 1970 album Psychedelic Shack, but Motown refused to release it as their single for fear of the group's image - so Whitfield re-recorded it with Edwin Starr, whose June 1970 Gordy single went to No. 1.

songs.title: When the Levee Breaks
songs.originalArtist: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
songs.writer: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
songs.whyNotable: One of the most sampled drum tracks in music history is a 1971 rearrangement of a Delta blues record cut in June 1929. Zeppelin's version credits Memphis Minnie alongside the band; McCoy, whom Charles Shaar Murray identifies as the actual songwriter, is not on the Zeppelin credit.

songs.title: You Are My Sunshine
songs.writer: Credited to Jimmie Davis and Charles Mitchell (authorship disputed)
songs.whyNotable: The Pine Ridge Boys recorded it 22 August 1939 and Bluebird released it 6 October 1939, with no songwriter listed; the Rice Brothers' Gang cut it for Decca on 13 September 1939. Davis did not record it until 5 February 1940, after buying the rights from Paul Rice - yet he is universally treated as both author and first recorder.

songs.title: You Don't Have to Say You Love Me
songs.writer: Pino Donaggio and Vito Pallavicini (original); Vicki Wickham and Simon Napier-Bell (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: Donaggio debuted 'Io che non vivo (senza te)' at the 1965 Sanremo Festival and took it to No. 1 in Italy that March. Springfield, who heard it at Sanremo, taped her English version in London on 9-10 March 1966.

songs.title: You Got the Love
songs.writer: Anthony B. Stephens, Arnecia Michelle Harris and John Bellamy
songs.whyNotable: A pure TV-sync case. The Source featuring Candi Staton released it in 1986; Florence + the Machine's 2009 Island version was carried into mass awareness by the Gossip Girl and Gavin & Stacey finales and Sky Sports football coverage, and a large cohort has never encountered the 1986 record at all.

songs.title: Baby, Please Don't Go
songs.writer: Traditional (Joe Williams credited on the record)
songs.whyNotable: Big Joe Williams cut it in Chicago on 31 October 1935, billed as Joe Williams' Washboard Blues Singers. Them's October 1964 Decca recording with the 19-year-old Van Morrison is now treated as definitive, and AC/DC's 1975 version added another layer.

songs.title: Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)
songs.whyNotable: Cher recorded it first, on 11 February 1966, released later that month on Imperial. Nancy Sinatra's cover from the same year was placed over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1, and post-Tarantino audiences overwhelmingly treat the Sinatra recording as the original.

songs.title: Both Sides, Now
songs.originalArtist: Dave Van Ronk and the Hudson Dusters
songs.whyNotable: Mitchell wrote it, but she was the third act to put it on record: Dave Van Ronk and the Hudson Dusters released it as 'Clouds' in June 1967 and Judy Collins cut it for Wildflowers the same year. Mitchell's own recording did not appear until the 1969 Reprise album Clouds.

songs.title: Cups (When I'm Gone)
songs.writer: A.P. Carter (1931 song); cup arrangement by Heloise Tunstall-Behrens and Luisa Gerstein
songs.whyNotable: Kendrick's Pitch Perfect version is assumed original, but the viral cup arrangement was created by Lulu and the Lampshades (2009) atop A.P. Carter's 1931 folk song.

songs.title: Everything I Own
songs.whyNotable: In Britain the song reads as a reggae standard thanks to Ken Boothe's 1974 UK No. 1 and Boy George's 1987 number one, but David Gates wrote it for Bread as an elegy for his father and their version charted in the US in 1972.

songs.title: Feeling Good
songs.whyNotable: Written for the 1964 musical 'The Roar of the Greasepaint' and first performed by Cy Grant; assumed to originate with Simone's 1965 (or Bublé's 2005) version.

songs.title: Fever
songs.whyNotable: Peggy Lee's 1958 rearrangement became her signature, overshadowing Little Willie John's 1956 R&B original.

songs.title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon
songs.whyNotable: Neil Diamond wrote and first recorded it, released March 1967 on Bang. Urge Overkill's version, cut for their 1992 EP Stull, became the definitive one for a generation after its use in Pulp Fiction - many viewers meet it as an Urge Overkill song with no idea a 1967 original exists.

songs.title: Hallelujah
songs.whyNotable: Cohen's authorship is fairly well known, but Buckley's 1994 version is so dominant many believe his recording is the original.

songs.title: I Will Always Love You
songs.whyNotable: Parton wrote and first recorded it (1973-74); Houston's 1992 Bodyguard version leads many to assume it was written for her.

songs.title: Iko Iko
songs.originalArtist: James "Sugar Boy" Crawford and His Cane Cutters
songs.whyNotable: First recorded in November 1953 as 'Jock-A-Mo' by James 'Sugar Boy' Crawford on Checker. The Dixie Cups' March 1965 Red Bird version renamed it and is treated as the source; the Belle Stars' 1982 cover charted in the US only after Rain Man, adding a third generation of confusion.

songs.title: Killing Me Softly with His Song
songs.whyNotable: Lori Lieberman recorded it first (1972), Roberta Flack made it a 1973 standard; a generation knows only the Fugees' 1996 version.

songs.title: Let It Be Me
songs.writer: Gilbert Bécaud (music) and Pierre Delanoë (French lyrics); Manny Curtis (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The song began as the French 'Je t'appartiens', sung by Bécaud and released as an HMV single in 1955. Jill Corey sang the first English version on television in 1957; the Everly Brothers recorded theirs in December 1959, and Cadence released it in 1960.

songs.title: Mad World
songs.whyNotable: The stark 2003 Jules/Andrews piano version leads many younger listeners to think it's the original, not a slowed reworking of a 1982 Tears for Fears hit.

songs.title: Mas que Nada
songs.whyNotable: Jorge Ben recorded his own song on his 1963 Philips debut Samba Esquema Novo. Mendes' 1966 Brasil '66 version is so dominant outside Brazil that it is widely treated as definitive.

songs.title: Money (That's What I Want)
songs.whyNotable: Barrett Strong's 1959 Tamla single became Motown's first hit in June 1960; the Beatles' 1963 closer on With the Beatles is the version most listeners meet first. The Rolling Stones cut it too, in January 1964.

songs.title: Monkey Man
songs.whyNotable: A staple of the Specials' 1979 debut and widely taken for a 2 Tone original, it is Toots Hibbert's 1969 Leslie Kong-produced single, a modest UK No. 47 whose British fame arrived a decade later.

songs.title: Mr. Bojangles
songs.whyNotable: Walker wrote it about a street performer he met in a New Orleans jail and cut it at Phillips Recording in Memphis, released by Atco on 20 June 1968; the Dirt Band's 1970 recording became a No. 9 hit in 1971, and Sammy Davis Jr.'s 1972 showpiece muddies the attribution further.

songs.title: Need Your Love So Bad
songs.writer: Mertis John Jr. and William Edward John
songs.whyNotable: Little Willie John released it on King on 20 October 1955 and it reached No. 5 on the Billboard R&B chart in 1956. Peter Green's string-laden Blue Horizon single from July 1968 is the version British audiences know, and it is routinely assumed to be a Fleetwood Mac original.

songs.title: Rollin' and Tumblin'
songs.whyNotable: Even blues listeners name Muddy Waters, who cut it in 1950, but the first recording was made in Atlanta on 14 March 1929 by the near-forgotten Hambone Willie Newbern for Okeh. Cream's 1966 Fresh Cream version added a third layer for rock audiences.

songs.title: Take Me to the River
songs.whyNotable: Al Green co-wrote and first recorded it on Al Green Explores Your Mind in 1974, but Hi Records never issued his version as a single - it released Syl Johnson's 1975 cover instead. Talking Heads' 1978 Sire single reached No. 26 and is often taken for the source.

songs.title: The Man Who Sold the World
songs.whyNotable: Bowie's 1970 original is a deep cut; after Nirvana's 1993 Unplugged version many younger fans credited the song to Nirvana.

songs.title: Turn! Turn! Turn!
songs.whyNotable: Seeger wrote it in 1959, but the first released recording was the Limeliters' 'To Everything There Is a Season' on their 1962 RCA Victor album Folk Matinee, ahead of Seeger's own version that same year; the Byrds' October 1965 Columbia single went to No. 1 and owns the song publicly.

songs.title: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes
songs.whyNotable: María Grever's Spanish song 'Cuando vuelva a tu lado' was written and first recorded in 1934, by Orquesta Pedro Vía. Washington's 1959 Mercury single won a Grammy and is treated as the song's origin point, twenty-five years late.

songs.title: Higher Ground
songs.whyNotable: Stevie Wonder's 1973 Innervisions classic is well known, but many rock-era listeners assume the 1989 RHCP version originated it.
songs.dropReason: No documentable public belief RHCP originated it; Stevie Wonder original is a #4 pop/#1 R&B hit, RHCP version widely known AS a cover.

songs.title: (I Can't Help) Falling in Love with You
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar comprehensively. UB40's 1993 version was enormous, but the Elvis Presley original is one of the best-known recordings in popular music and nobody mistakes the attribution.

songs.title: (Your Love Keeps Lifting Me) Higher and Higher
songs.dropReason: Rita Coolidge's March 1977 A&M version reached number 2, but Jackie Wilson's July 1967 Brunswick original (number 6 pop, number 1 R&B) is the better-remembered record today. There is no meaningful body of belief that Coolidge originated it — the confusion runs the other way if anywhere.

songs.title: 99 Luftballons / Falling in Love Again
songs.dropReason: Not covers in the scope sense — Nena and Marlene Dietrich each recorded both the German and English versions of their own songs. There is no covering act to be mistaken for the original recorder.

songs.title: Act Naturally
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Buck Owens and the Buckaroos recorded it 12 February 1963 and released it 11 March 1963 on Capitol, taking it to No. 1 country; the Beatles cut it 17 June 1965 for Help!. But the Beatles' early cover repertoire is exhaustively documented and this track is routinely labelled a Buck Owens cover — the honest rating is low, not medium.

songs.title: Ain't No Mountain High Enough
songs.dropReason: Same precedent. Diana Ross's July 1970 Motown version was a three-week number one, but Marvin Gaye & Tammi Terrell's April 1967 Tamla original is universally credited to them and is if anything the more culturally present record now. Verified; no earlier recording exists than theirs.

songs.title: Ain't No Mountain High Enough (Diana Ross / Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell)
songs.dropReason: Explicitly excluded by the vein: Ross's version was already a straight No. 1 chart hit long before Guardians of the Galaxy or Remember the Titans. The sync did not drive the misattribution, it inherited one. May belong to a chart-displacement vein instead.

songs.title: Always on My Mind
songs.dropReason: Vein mismatch plus a muddy origin. The first recording (Brenda Lee) is country-pop and the first release (Gwen McCrae, March 1972) is soul; the strongest public misbelief credits Willie Nelson, which is country→country. Genuinely interesting provenance — logged in contested for a different vein.
caveats: researched and NOT returned (vein mismatch; see dropped). The provenance is genuinely tangled: first RECORDED by Brenda Lee (released June 1972, Decca), first RELEASED by Gwen McCrae as 'You Were Always on My Mind' on 28 March 1972 (Columbia). Elvis recorded 29 March 1972 and released 31 October 1972; Willie Nelson February 1982; Pet Shop Boys 30 November 1987. Four separate acts are each widely believed to have originated it.

songs.title: Autumn Leaves
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. It is understood as a standard rather than any one act's song — no single cover act is popularly mistaken for the originator. The French provenance (Kosma/Prévert, "Les Feuilles mortes", 1945) is also broadly known. Kept in contested for the Vaucaire/Montand ordering.
caveats: dropped, but the record is contested and worth noting for a future harvest. Wikipedia calls Yves Montand's 1949 Columbia recording of "Les Feuilles mortes" the most successful French version, but Cora Vaucaire recorded it around 1947–48, earlier. Jo Stafford made "the first English-language recording in July, 1950."

songs.title: Bam Bam
songs.dropReason: Could not verify — the Wikipedia article at the expected URL returned 404, so the relationship between Toots and the Maytals' 1966 Festival-winning song and Sister Nancy's 1982 record is unconfirmed. It also sits awkwardly in the vein: both acts are Jamaican, so there is no pop cover act being mistaken for the original recording artist, and Sister Nancy's may be a derivation on a shared riddim rather than a cover.

songs.title: Bei Mir Bistu Shein
songs.dropReason: No pre-Andrews Sisters RECORDING is documented. Wikipedia establishes the 1932 Yiddish stage origin (Secunda/Jacobs, Parkway Theatre, Brooklyn) and the Andrews Sisters' 24 November 1937 Decca session, but says only that other artists covered it within thirty days AFTER them. Searching surfaced a 1937 Apollo Theater performance in Yiddish by Johnnie and George that Sammy Cahn heard — a performance, not a record. Scope requires who recorded it first; unmeetable.

songs.title: Bésame Mucho
songs.dropReason: Wikipedia does not name a first recording artist. It gives the 1932 composition date (Consuelo Velázquez), a 1940 release year in the infobox with no artist, and the charting English versions (Jimmy Dorsey number one US 1944, Andy Russell number eight 1944, the Coasters number 70 in 1960). Cannot state originalArtist.

songs.title: Betcha by Golly, Wow
songs.dropReason: Structurally misleading. Connie Stevens did record Thom Bell and Linda Creed's song first, for Bell in 1970 — but under the title 'Keep Growing Strong'. The Stylistics WERE the first to record it as 'Betcha by Golly, Wow' (Avco, February 17, 1972), so a page hung on this title would assert something false. Good contested trivia, bad candidate.

songs.title: Black Betty (Ram Jam / Lead Belly)
songs.dropReason: Fails the sync test and I could not source it. Ram Jam's was a charting single in its own right, and the advert/stadium revival that followed cannot be pinned to a specific documented placement the way Bravia or Wednesday can.

songs.title: Blue Bayou
songs.dropReason: Direction of travel is wrong for this vein: Roy Orbison's pop original later made famous by Linda Ronstadt's country-rock reading. The brief explicitly routes pop-original→country-cover elsewhere.

songs.title: Blue Moon of Kentucky
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Bill Monroe wrote it and recorded it with the Blue Grass Boys on 16 September 1946 (Columbia, released early 1947); Elvis cut it at Sun on 7 July 1954. But Monroe's ownership of the song is one of the best-known facts in bluegrass and it is universally presented as the B-side cover on Elvis's first single. Everyone who cares already knows.

songs.title: Blue Velvet (Bobby Vinton / Tony Bennett)
songs.dropReason: Vinton's version was a chart-topping hit years before David Lynch's film, so the film cannot be what drove the misattribution. Belongs to a different vein if anywhere.

songs.title: Boom Boom
songs.dropReason: John Lee Hooker's original is the definitive and universally credited version. The Animals' reading is understood as a cover. No confusion to document.

songs.title: Born Under a Bad Sign
songs.dropReason: Albert King's 1967 Stax recording is itself a canonical, widely known record and the Cream version is presented as a cover of it. Also the axis would drift toward the writing credit (Booker T. Jones and William Bell) rather than first recording.

songs.title: Bring It On Home to Me
songs.dropReason: Sam Cooke's original is one of the best-known soul records ever made and is never mistaken for anyone else's. The Animals' version is plainly a cover. (Note: distinct from "Bring It On Home", already in the corpus.)

songs.title: Brown Girl in the Ring
songs.dropReason: Unverifiable original. Boney M.'s 1978 version draws on a Jamaican children's ring game with no identifiable first recording, so there is no original recording artist to name and the required axis cannot be established.

songs.title: Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White
songs.dropReason: Wikipedia says the song "was first recorded and released in Mexico in 1953" as "Cerezo Rosa" but names no artist for that recording, and names no recording of Louiguy's 1950 French original "Cerisiers Roses et Pommiers Blancs". Pérez Prado's RCA Victor instrumental (recorded 23 August 1954, ten weeks at number one in 1955) is the famous version, but I cannot fill originalArtist.

songs.title: Dancing in the Street
songs.dropReason: Bowie/Jagger 1985 and Van Halen 1982 are both plainly understood as covers; Martha and the Vandellas' 1964 original is universally credited.

songs.title: Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood (The Animals / Nina Simone)
songs.dropReason: Fails the sync test. The Animals' version was a large chart hit in 1965, long before the Santa Esmeralda reading in Kill Bill. The Simone-first fact is genuinely interesting but belongs to a chart-displacement vein, not this one.

songs.title: Dust My Broom
songs.dropReason: Better as a footnote than a page. The Elmore James / Robert Johnson relationship is a genuine priority question, but the covering-rock-act misattribution the site is built on is not present — no rock act is credibly believed to have originated it.

songs.title: Enjoy Yourself (It's Later Than You Think)
songs.dropReason: Confusion too weak. Written by Carl Sigman and Herb Magidson, first recorded by Guy Lombardo and His Royal Canadians on 27–28 November 1949 for Decca, charting from 13 January 1950 and peaking at number 10 — a widely known pre-rock standard that Doris Day, Bing Crosby, Tommy Dorsey, Louis Prima and the Supremes also cut. The Specials' 1980 version opens and closes More Specials but, per Wikipedia, was never released as a single from it. Nobody credible thinks a 2 Tone band wrote a 1949 pop standard.

songs.title: Gentle on My Mind
songs.dropReason: Two failures. The gap is one month (John Hartford, RCA, May 1967 → Glen Campbell, June 1967), and Hartford's authorship is prominent enough that he won a Grammy for the song in 1968 alongside Campbell. Also a country/folk→country-pop move rather than a pop/rock cover.

songs.title: Get Ready / Take Me in Your Arms (Rock Me a Little While)
songs.dropReason: Both are legitimate Motown same-label re-cuts (Rare Earth 1970; Isley Brothers 1968 and Doobie Brothers 1975), but the covering versions are not salient enough today for anyone to believe they came first. No confusion to document.

songs.title: Guantanamera
songs.dropReason: Wikipedia: "it is unclear when the first release as a record occurred." No originalArtist obtainable. Confusion would have been medium at best anyway — Pete Seeger's version is described as definitive and the Sandpipers' 1966 hit (number nine US, number seven UK) is broadly understood as a Cuban song.
caveats: unusable as written because Wikipedia states "it is unclear when the first release as a record occurred." Joseíto Fernández is credited as writer and "first popularized the song on radio as early as 1929", but radio popularisation is not a recording. Do not let a future harvest turn the 1929 radio date into a recording date.

songs.title: Guns of Navarone
songs.dropReason: Too tangled and the confusion is weak. The Skatalites' 1965 ska instrumental is itself an adaptation of Dimitri Tiomkin's 1961 film theme, and The Specials' version was a live recording rather than a studio single — a three-way instrumental derivation, not a clean cover mistaken for an original.

songs.title: Have You Seen Her / Everybody Plays the Fool
songs.dropReason: MC Hammer (1990) and Aaron Neville (1991) are real cover-mistaken-for-original cases, but the originals sit on Brunswick and RCA rather than the vein's labels and the confusion is thinner than the keepers'. Parked rather than padded out the list.

songs.title: Hazy Shade of Winter (The Bangles / Simon and Garfunkel, Less Than Zero)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Genuine film-driven cover, but there is no documentable public belief that the Bangles originated it — Simon and Garfunkel's version is too familiar.

songs.title: Help Me Make It Through the Night
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. John Holt's reggae version is well known, but Kris Kristofferson's authorship and Sammi Smith's hit recording are securely and widely attributed.

songs.title: Hot Hot Hot
songs.dropReason: Out of vein. Arrow's original and Buster Poindexter's cover are soca, not reggae, ska or rocksteady, and the vein is scoped to Jamaican studio traditions. Flagging it here so a future soca or calypso vein can pick it up rather than losing it.

songs.title: Hush (Deep Purple / Billy Joe Royal)
songs.dropReason: Fails the sync test. Deep Purple's version was a US top-five hit on release; no film or advert drove the confusion.

songs.title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine (Marvin Gaye / Gladys Knight and the Pips / Smokey Robinson, California Raisins adverts)
songs.dropReason: Fails the sync test. Gaye's was a No. 1 before the adverts existed; the campaign revived an already-dominant recording rather than creating the misattribution. The Knight/Robinson ordering question is a different vein.

songs.title: I Say a Little Prayer (Aretha Franklin / Dionne Warwick)
songs.dropReason: Same failure. Aretha's version was a US top-ten hit in 1968, decades before My Best Friend's Wedding made it a film standard. The sync amplified an existing confusion rather than creating it.

songs.title: I Shot the Sheriff
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar on the Higher Ground precedent. Bob Marley wrote it and recorded it first, on Burnin' in 1973, and the song is universally credited to him; Clapton's 1974 version from 461 Ocean Boulevard is famously known AS a cover, which is most of its cultural meaning. The Wikipedia article documents no public confusion about who originated it. This is the canonical reggae cover and it will be proposed again — it should not be.

songs.title: I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing (The New Seekers / The Hillside Singers, Coca-Cola advert)
songs.dropReason: Advert-origin, but the direction of the claim is muddled — the Coca-Cola jingle preceded both full-length records rather than one act covering another's release. Not a clean cover-misattribution and I would have had to assert an ordering I could not cleanly source.

songs.title: I'd Rather Go Blind
songs.dropReason: Etta James's 1968 Chess original is universally credited; the Chicken Shack and Rod Stewart versions are known as covers.

songs.title: If I Were a Carpenter
songs.dropReason: Not a misattribution at all. Bobby Darin's Atlantic version was released in September 1966, before Tim Hardin's own recording appeared on Tim Hardin 2 (1967, Verve Forecast). Darin genuinely got there first on record, so crediting him is not an error.

songs.title: If You Go Away
songs.dropReason: Wikipedia does not identify who recorded the first English version, so originalArtist is unobtainable. Confusion is also weak — the Brel provenance of "Ne me quitte pas" (1959) is widely known and none of Dusty Springfield (1967), Scott Walker (1969) or Terry Jacks (1974) is taken for the originator.

songs.title: It Must Be Love (Madness / Labi Siffre)
songs.dropReason: Fails the sync test. High confusion, but Madness's version was a straight chart hit and no film, TV or advert placement drove it. Worth harvesting under a different vein.

songs.title: It's Oh So Quiet (Björk / Betty Hutton)
songs.dropReason: Excellent confusion and a superb contested chain back through Betty Hutton to a German-language original, but no sync drove it — Björk's version rose on its own single release and music video. Should be harvested under a different vein.

songs.title: It's Raining Men (Geri Halliwell / The Weather Girls, Bridget Jones's Diary)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. The Weather Girls' original is instantly recognisable and still in constant rotation.

songs.title: Johnny Too Bad
songs.dropReason: Dropped on unconfirmable dates, per the vein's explicit instruction. Wikipedia gives no year for the Slickers' original single — only that it appeared on the 1972 soundtrack to The Harder They Come — and gives no year at all for the UB40 or Taj Mahal versions, noting only that they appeared on compilations. Jim Capaldi's 1975 version and John Martyn's from 1980 are dated, but neither is the cover that would drive the misattribution.

songs.title: Jolene / Big Yellow Taxi / Mr. Tambourine Man / Blowin' in the Wind
songs.dropReason: Famous-cover cases where the original is at least as famous as the cover. Nobody thinks the White Stripes, Counting Crows, the Byrds or Peter, Paul and Mary originated these. Dropped on the confusion bar without further research.

songs.title: Just a Gigolo
songs.dropReason: Same problem. Wikipedia documents 1929 publication and German orchestral performances of "Schöner Gigolo, armer Gigolo" (Casucci/Brammer) but no first recording; the earliest dated recording on the page is Leo Reisman, 5 January 1931, in English. Confusion would be high (Louis Prima 1956, David Lee Roth 1985, number 12 Hot 100) if the original recorder could be pinned down.
caveats: the German original's first recording is not established on Wikipedia. The article says the song "was first published by Wiener Boheme Verlag in 1929 and performed by several orchestras in Germany that year, including Dajos Béla's orchestra with the singer Kurt Mühlhardt" — performed, not recorded. The earliest DATED recording anywhere on the page is Leo Reisman and His Orchestra, 5 January 1931 (Victor 22606), an English-language version. A search snippet asserted a 1929 Dajos Béla recording but that claim does not appear in the article text. Dropped for now; strong if someone can source the 1929 German disc.

songs.title: Killing Floor
songs.dropReason: Howlin' Wolf's 1960s Chess original is well credited and the Hendrix / Electric Flag readings are known as covers. No misattribution to the covering act.

songs.title: Knockin' on Heaven's Door (Guns N' Roses / Bob Dylan)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Universally known as a Dylan song.

songs.title: La Bamba
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Los Lobos' 1987 version is famously a cover, released as the title track of a Ritchie Valens biopic — the film itself tells the audience it is Valens's record. Nothing to correct.

songs.title: Let's Stay Together
songs.dropReason: Tina Turner's 1983 comeback single is known as a cover, and Al Green's 1971 Hi original is iconic and universally credited.

songs.title: Little Red Rooster
songs.dropReason: The textbook case the vein warning describes. The Rolling Stones' November 1964 single is famous precisely AS a blues cover — Wikipedia notes it remains the only blues song ever to top the British pop charts, and that framing travels with it. Howlin' Wolf's June 1961 Chess original is well credited, and Sam Cooke's 1963 version (No. 7 R&B, No. 11 pop) sits in between. No genuine public belief that the Stones originated it.
caveats: dropped as a candidate, but the antecedent chain is strong: Charley Patton's "Banty Rooster Blues" (1929) shares verses and Memphis Minnie's "If You See My Rooster (Please Run Him Home)" (1936) shares melody lines. Separately, Margie Day recorded an unrelated jump-blues "Little Red Rooster" for Dot in 1950 which reached No. 5 on Billboard's R&B retail chart in 1951 — a title collision, not a version.

songs.title: Long Black Veil
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion axis. Written by Danny Dill and Marijohn Wilkin and first recorded by Lefty Frizzell (recorded 3 March 1959, released 20 April 1959, Columbia). It IS widely mistaken for a traditional folk ballad — Dill called it an 'instant folksong' — but no specific cover act (The Band, Cash, Baez, Nick Cave) is credited with originating it. 'Mistaken for traditional' is a different claim than 'this act is mistaken for the original recorder'.

songs.title: Long Shot Kick de Bucket / Skinhead Moonstomp / Too Hot
songs.dropReason: All dropped for insufficient public profile on the covering side. In each case both the original and the cover are known mainly to ska specialists, so there is no broad public belief to correct — the confusion bar requires a mistaken mass audience, not an obscure pairing.

songs.title: Love in Vain
songs.dropReason: The Rolling Stones credited Robert Johnson and the connection is part of the standard Let It Bleed commentary. Johnson's authorship and priority are widely understood — famous AS a cover.

songs.title: Mack the Knife
songs.dropReason: Fails the sourcing rule, not the confusion bar. Confusion is high (Bobby Darin, Atco, 1959) but Wikipedia names no first recording of the 1928 German original — only an undated "cast recording" and an undated Sidney Bechet version, plus Louis Armstrong 1955 as the first to reach the US hit parade with a vocal version. I will not assert an originalArtist I could not verify. See contested.
caveats: I could NOT confirm a first recording and have therefore dropped it rather than guess. The Wikipedia article names no first recording of the German original: it says only that "A number of early artists recorded the song, including the cast recording and a jazz version by Sidney Bechet, but it was Louis Armstrong who first introduced the vocal version of 'Mack the Knife' to the United States hit parade" (recorded 28 September 1955, released November 1955). No dates are given for the cast recording or the Bechet version, and The Threepenny Opera page names Kurt Gerron as the Street Singer at the Berlin premiere on 31 August 1928 but identifies no 1928 or 1929 recordings. Search results variously claimed Harald Paulsen (1928) and Bertolt Brecht (1929) as the first record, but these came from blogs and wikis, not a source I could verify. A researchable page is here if someone reads a discography — the confusion (everyone says Bobby Darin, 1958 session, 1959 Atco release) is as high as it gets.

songs.title: Many Rivers to Cross
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. Jimmy Cliff wrote and recorded it and is universally credited; the UB40, Joe Cocker and Annie Lennox versions are all plainly understood as covers of a Jimmy Cliff song.

songs.title: Nature Boy (David Bowie / Nat King Cole, Moulin Rouge!)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Nat King Cole's 1948 recording is iconic and the Bowie version is understood as an interpretation.

songs.title: Nel blu, dipinto di blu (Volare)
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar outright. Modugno's own Fonit original was itself the American hit — five non-consecutive weeks at number one on the Hot 100 in 1958 and Billboard's number one single of the year. Dean Martin's version peaked at number 15 US. The original is the famous one; there is nothing to correct.

songs.title: Non, je ne regrette rien
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Piaf's 1960 recording is the original and is universally credited to her; no cover act is taken for the originator.

songs.title: Not Fade Away
songs.dropReason: Buddy Holly's original is too famous to be displaced; the Rolling Stones' 1964 single is understood as a Holly cover and is routinely discussed that way.

songs.title: Ol' 55
songs.dropReason: Medium at best and the weakest of the singer-songwriter→rock set. Tom Waits wrote and recorded it for Closing Time (March 1973, Asylum); the Eagles covered it on On the Border (1974). Waits's authorship stayed visible — partly because he publicly disliked the Eagles' version — so the provenance was never really lost. Held back rather than padding the list.

songs.title: One Day I'll Fly Away (Nicole Kidman / Randy Crawford, Moulin Rouge!)
songs.dropReason: Same film as the Lady Marmalade keeper but much weaker: no documentable belief that the film version is the original, and the placement did not produce a hit single.

songs.title: People Are Strange (Echo and the Bunnymen / The Doors, The Lost Boys)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. The Doors' original is universally known; the cover reads as a cover.

songs.title: Perhaps, Perhaps, Perhaps (Doris Day / Bobby Capó, Coupling)
songs.dropReason: Dropped on research grounds. It is an English adaptation of the Spanish 'Quizás, Quizás, Quizás', so the who-recorded-it-first axis is confounded by translation, and I found no documentable public belief that Doris Day originated it.

songs.title: Please Mr. Postman
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar on the Higher Ground precedent. The Marvelettes' August 1961 Tamla original was the first Motown number one on the Hot 100 and is universally credited to them, and the Carpenters' 1974 number one is famously known AS an oldies remake. Verified (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Please_Mr._Postman) but not proposed.

songs.title: Popcorn (Hot Butter / Gershon Kingsley)
songs.dropReason: No film, TV or advert placement drove the cover's dominance, so it fails the vein even though the confusion is high.

songs.title: Pressure Drop
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. Toots Hibbert wrote it and the Maytals recorded it in 1969, produced by Leslie Kong, released on Beverley's and Trojan in 1970, and Toots is universally credited — Rolling Stone placed the original at 453 on its 500 Greatest Songs list. The Clash, Robert Palmer, The Specials, Keith Richards and Izzy Stradlin versions are all understood as covers. No documentable belief that any covering act originated it.

songs.title: Rescue Me
songs.dropReason: Off-axis. The real, documented confusion is that listeners think Aretha Franklin sings Fontella Bass's 1965 Checker record — that is a mistaken identification of the singer on the original, not a covering act being mistaken for the originator. The locked scope does not cover it.

songs.title: Ring of Fire
songs.dropReason: Vein mismatch on the same grounds — the earlier recording and the famous one are both country. No pop/rock cover act is in the frame.

songs.title: Route 66
songs.dropReason: Trimmed as the weakest keeper. The facts are clean — Bobby Troup wrote it in 1946 and the King Cole Trio recorded it first, released 22 April 1946 on Capitol, number three Race Records and number 11 pop — but the Rolling Stones' 1964 debut album is famously a record of blues and R&B covers, and Nat King Cole's ownership of the song is well established. Closer to "everyone knows it's a cover" than the bar allows.

songs.title: Sea of Love (Cat Power / Phil Phillips, Juno)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. The Cat Power placement is too marginal to have generated public belief that she originated it, and The Honeydrippers' hit sits in between.

songs.title: Sixteen Tons
songs.dropReason: Out of vein and borderline on scope framing — it is a 1946 country/folk original (Merle Travis) rather than a standards, jazz or foreign-language one. Better suited to a country or folk vein; did not verify it here rather than stretch this one.

songs.title: Skinny Love (Birdy / Bon Iver)
songs.dropReason: No single sync drove it, so it fails the vein test. Wikipedia attributes the cover's rise to X Factor auditions in Australia (2012) and New Zealand (2013) plus its own chart run (No. 2 in five territories, No. 17 UK); the TV placements listed are scattered and split between both versions. Bon Iver's original is well known in its own right.

songs.title: Smokestack Lightning
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar in the other direction. Howlin' Wolf's is the version everybody knows; the Yardbirds' is the one heard as a cover. Nobody thinks the Yardbirds originated it.

songs.title: Somewhere Only We Know (Lily Allen / Keane, John Lewis Christmas advert)
songs.dropReason: Failed the confusion bar. The advert did drive the cover to No. 1 in the UK with over 600,000 sales, but Keane's 2004 Island original reached No. 3 and Wikipedia calls it 'Keane's signature composition'. Nobody genuinely believes Lily Allen originated it.

songs.title: Somewhere Over the Rainbow (Israel Kamakawiwo'ole / Judy Garland)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Heavily synced across ER, Scrubs and film, but Garland's is one of the most-recognised recordings ever made.

songs.title: Soul Man
songs.dropReason: The Blues Brothers' 1978 version is explicitly framed as tribute; Sam & Dave's Stax original is universally credited. Same failure mode as the already-ingested Blues Brothers case.

songs.title: Spanish Harlem
songs.dropReason: Aretha Franklin's 1971 version is large, but Ben E. King's 1960 Atco original is well enough credited that this sits below the bar. Borderline, dropped rather than padded.

songs.title: Spoonful
songs.dropReason: Cream's Fresh Cream version failed to chart on the Hot 100 and is discussed almost exclusively as a Howlin' Wolf / Willie Dixon blues being stretched out. Wolf's June 1960 Chess original is well credited. Fails the confusion bar for the same reason as Little Red Rooster.
caveats: Willie Dixon's 1960 song has documented antecedents: Papa Charlie Jackson's "All I Want Is a Spoonful" (1925), Luke Jordan (1927) and Charley Patton's "A Spoonful Blues" (1929). Dropped as a candidate on confusion grounds, but the lineage is the interesting part.

songs.title: Stand By Me / Bring It On Home to Me / Wonderful World
songs.dropReason: Ben E. King and Sam Cooke originals are among the best-credited records in soul. Every later version — Lennon, Herman's Hermits, the Animals — reads unambiguously as a cover.

songs.title: Stir It Up
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. Bob Marley composed it in 1967 and the Wailers recorded it that year; Johnny Nash's March 1972 Epic single reached number 12 US and 13 UK and was the first Marley-written song to succeed outside Jamaica, but the song today is universally a Marley song. The interesting fact — that the famous 1973 Catch a Fire version is itself a re-recording of a 1967 single — is a same-artist point, not the recorded-it-first axis this vertical is about.

songs.title: Such Great Heights (Iron and Wine / The Postal Service, Garden State)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. A real Garden State sync, but The Postal Service's original is well known to the same audience; the belief is not documentable.

songs.title: Summertime
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Universally understood as Gershwin, from Porgy and Bess (1935). Janis Joplin's version is not mistaken for an original.

songs.title: Summertime Blues
songs.dropReason: Eddie Cochran's original is a rock-and-roll standard in its own right; The Who's and Blue Cheer's versions are known as covers of it.

songs.title: Sweet Sensation
songs.dropReason: Could not establish documentable public belief that UB40 originated it. The Melodians' original is obscure enough to make the mechanism plausible, but plausibility is not evidence, and the Labour of Love series is generally known to be covers. Kingston Town and Red Red Wine from the same series are already in the corpus.

songs.title: Tears of a Clown
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. The Beat's 2 Tone version is a well-known cover of a Motown record universally credited to Smokey Robinson and the Miracles.

songs.title: The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face
songs.dropReason: Potentially strong — Roberta Flack's Atlantic recording versus Ewan MacColl's 1957 composition and the earliest folk recording of it — but NOT verified this pass, and the vein direction is inverted. Left for a folk-vein harvest rather than asserted here.

songs.title: The Gambler
songs.dropReason: Vein mismatch. Country original (Bobby Bare, 1978) covered by a country act (Kenny Rogers, November 1978). The confusion is enormous, but the direction of travel is country→country, not country→pop/rock. Belongs to a different vein.
caveats: researched and NOT returned (vein mismatch). Don Schlitz wrote it in August 1976; Bobby Bare recorded it first, in 1978 on the album Bare, and Johnny Cash also recorded it in 1978 on Gone Girl — both before Kenny Rogers' 15 November 1978 United Artists single. Public belief that Rogers originated it is near-total.

songs.title: The Harder They Come
songs.dropReason: Fails the confusion bar. Jimmy Cliff's original is inseparable from the 1972 film of the same name that he starred in; no cover is mistaken for it.

songs.title: The Lemon Song
songs.dropReason: Out of scope, same shape as Whole Lotta Love. Zeppelin's recording is the original recording under that title; the Howlin' Wolf connection ("Killing Floor") is a derivation and songwriting-credit matter, not a question of who recorded this title first.

songs.title: The Sound of Silence (Disturbed / Simon and Garfunkel)
songs.dropReason: Confusion bar. Simon and Garfunkel's original is one of the best-known records in popular music and the Disturbed version is famously discussed AS a cover. Same reasoning as the Higher Ground precedent.

songs.title: The Way You Do the Things You Do / Here I Am (Come and Take Me) / Homely Girl
songs.dropReason: All fail the confusion bar for the same reason: the originals — the Temptations, Al Green and the Chi-Lites respectively — are canonical, correctly attributed soul records, and Labour of Love II is widely understood as a covers album.

songs.title: Tom Dooley
songs.dropReason: Borderline, held back. G. B. Grayson and Henry Whitter recorded it for Victor in 1929 and Wikipedia notes several earlier recordings still; the Kingston Trio's 19 November 1958 Capitol single hit No. 1 and sold over six million. But the Kingston Trio were understood at the time and since as folk revivalists performing traditional material, which weakens the claim that they are mistaken for its originators.

songs.title: Walk This Way
songs.dropReason: Reverse direction and out of scope. Aerosmith recorded it first; the Run-DMC record is a famous collaboration and is universally known as a remake, not mistaken for the original.

songs.title: Whiskey in the Jar
songs.dropReason: No defensible originalArtist. Metallica (1999) covered Thin Lizzy's 1972 arrangement, and Thin Lizzy were not first either — the trail runs back through The Dubliners (1967), The Highwaymen (1962) and field recordings from 1940 to a 17th-century traditional. The scope requires naming who recorded it first, and no source supports a single name.
caveats: researched and NOT returned. A 17th-century traditional Irish ballad; documented field recordings run from Lena Bourne Fish (1940) through Séamus Ennis (Alan Lomax, 1951), with The Highwaymen releasing a version in 1962. The Dubliners recorded 1967, Thin Lizzy released 3 November 1972 (No. 1 Ireland, No. 6 UK), Metallica 1 February 1999 on Garage Inc. Metallica covered Thin Lizzy's arrangement, not the traditional — so the 'original recording artist' axis has no single defensible answer, which is why it was held back rather than harvested.

songs.title: Whole Lotta Love
songs.dropReason: Out of scope. Led Zeppelin's 1969 recording IS the first recording of a song by that title. The famous dispute is a songwriting/lyric-derivation claim against Willie Dixon's "You Need Love" — a different title, and per the locked scope a writing claim, not a first-recording claim.

songs.title: Wild Horses
songs.dropReason: Fails the locked scope. The Flying Burrito Brothers RELEASED it first (Burrito Deluxe, April 1970), but the Rolling Stones RECORDED it first (2–4 December 1969, Muscle Shoals) and licensed it to Gram Parsons. The axis here is first release, not first recording. Kept in contested.
caveats: researched and NOT returned as a candidate. The Flying Burrito Brothers released it first, on Burrito Deluxe in April 1970, roughly a year before the Rolling Stones' June 1971 Sticky Fingers single. But the Stones RECORDED it first, on 2–4 December 1969 at Muscle Shoals, and licensed it to Gram Parsons on condition it not be a single. First release ≠ first recording, so it fails the locked scope — but it is a strong page for a 'first release' angle if the site ever opens one.
